notes.body: Zero trust is a set of design principles, not a product SKU. The core idea is simple and brutal: no user, device, application, or network segment is trusted by default — every access request is authenticated, authorized, and continuously re-evaluated. Location used to be trust. In the old castle-and-moat model, anything inside the corporate network was treated as friendly and anything outside as hostile. That model died the moment laptops left the building, VPNs became the front door, and attackers learned that phishing one employee puts them inside the moat. Zero trust moves the trust decision from 'where are you?' to 'who are you, what is the health of your device, and is this specific request legitimate right now?' NIST SP 800-207, the canonical reference, frames zero trust around a simple rule: all communication is secured regardless of network location, access is granted per session, and access decisions are driven by dynamic policy that considers client identity, the requesting asset's posture, and behavioral attributes. Notice what is missing from that list: 'because the request came from the office LAN.' There are three ideas people constantly confuse with zero trust, so let us separate them. First, zero trust is not 'no trust at all' — it is trust that is explicitly granted, narrowly scoped, and constantly re-verified. You still trust your identity provider, your policy engine, and your device health signals; you just stop trusting the network cable. Second, zero trust is not a firewall upgrade. A firewall is one enforcement point; zero trust is the architecture that coordinates all of them. Third, zero trust is not achieved by buying a platform — it is achieved by changing defaults: default-deny instead of default-allow, per-session authorization instead of login-once, and continuous diagnostics instead of annual audits. On the endpoint, the single most consequential default you can change is which applications are allowed to run. A default-allow endpoint runs whatever arrives; a default-deny endpoint runs only what policy explicitly permits. Everything ThreatLocker's allowlisting module does — and everything you will operate in this course — is zero trust applied to the question 'may this code execute on this machine?' Common operator gotcha: do not pitch zero trust to leadership or to an interview panel as a product. The panel on October 13 will respect you far more for saying 'zero trust is the discipline of removing implicit trust and enforcing per-session, policy-driven decisions, and here is how we applied it to application execution' than for naming vendors.
notes.title: What 'zero trust' actually means

notes.body: NIST SP 800-207 gives zero trust a logical anatomy with three named components, and you should be able to draw them from memory. The Policy Engine (PE) is the brain: it makes the ultimate decision to grant, deny, or revoke access to a resource, using enterprise policy plus inputs like identity, device posture, and threat intelligence. The Policy Administrator (PA) is the muscle that carries out the decision: it establishes and tears down the communication path between the subject and the resource, for example by generating session credentials or configuring the enforcement point. The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) is the gate: it sits in the data path, enables or terminates connections, and enforces the PE's decision. The PE and PA together form the control plane; the PEP and the resource sit in the data plane. A trust algorithm inside the PE weighs the inputs — identity assurance level, device compliance state, behavioral anomalies — and produces the decision. Worked example, mapped to an endpoint: an accountant double-clicks invoicing-app.exe. The endpoint agent acting as PEP intercepts the execution request instead of letting it run. It asks the control plane: the PE evaluates policy ('is invoicing-app.exe on the allowlist for the accounting group? is the device compliant? is the file hash unchanged?') and the PA instructs the PEP to allow or block the launch. If allowed, the PEP permits that specific execution; it does not hand the app a permanent hall pass. That is the per-session idea applied to process execution. Now map the failure modes, because operators live in failure modes. If the PEP is bypassed — the app launches without consulting policy — the whole model collapses regardless of how good the PE is. If the PE's inputs are stale — device posture from last week — decisions are made on lies. If the PA cannot reach the PEP — the agent is offline — you need a defined offline posture: fail closed (block new executions) or fail open, and you must choose deliberately, document it, and be able to defend the choice. Common gotcha: people draw the PE, PA, and PEP as three boxes and stop. The interview-grade understanding is the data flow between them and what happens when each link breaks. Practice explaining it in sixty seconds: subject requests, PEP intercepts, PE decides with the trust algorithm, PA enforces, PEP gates. Then add: 'and on the endpoint, the application-control agent is the PEP for the question of whether code may run.'
notes.title: NIST SP 800-207: the logical model (PE, PA, PEP)

notes.body: Every security control is either default-allow (permit unless explicitly blocked) or default-deny (block unless explicitly permitted), and the choice decides who does the hard work: the defender or the attacker. Default-allow puts the burden on the defender to enumerate badness. Antivirus signatures, blocklists, firewall deny rules — all of these require you to know about the threat in advance, name it, and push the rule before the threat arrives. The attacker only needs one thing you have not seen yet: a fresh hash, a new domain, a renamed binary. This is an asymmetric game you lose by construction, because the space of 'unknown bad' is infinite and your blocklist is finite. Default-deny flips the burden. The policy enumerates goodness — the finite, knowable set of applications your business actually uses — and everything else is denied without needing to be recognized. The attacker's novel malware is not blocked because it is known-bad; it is blocked because it is not known-good, which requires zero threat intelligence about that specific sample. Worked example: a finance team uses 40 applications. Under default-allow, the defender must maintain rules against millions of malware families and hope the next one is recognized. Under default-deny, the defender maintains 40 allow entries and the next malware fails at the gate unrecognized — which is fine, because recognition was never required. Now the honest costs, because default-deny is not free. First, someone must build and maintain the allowlist: discover what is used, approve it, handle updates. Second, the first weeks are noisy: legitimate apps get blocked and users complain, so you need a fast approval workflow or the business routes around you. Third, allowlisting the application is necessary but not sufficient — a trusted app can be abused, which is exactly why ringfencing exists (Module M03) and why you should never present allowlisting as the whole answer. The classic mistake is treating default-deny as 'set and forget.' It is a living policy: every software update changes hashes, every new hire needs new apps, every acquired company brings unknown software. Operator habit: measure your policy's health by the approval queue's age. A queue of pending approvals older than your SLA is not a backlog; it is users learning to work around security. In the interview, when they ask why ThreatLocker leads with allowlisting, the answer is this economics argument in two sentences: default-allow forces defenders to enumerate infinite badness; default-deny enumerates finite goodness, so unknown threats fail closed with no signature required.
notes.title: Default-allow vs default-deny: the economics of the two models

notes.body: Assume breach is the psychological core of zero trust: design as though the attacker is already inside. This is not pessimism; it is engineering discipline. If you assume the perimeter will fail — because it will, via phishing, a vendor compromise, or a zero-day — then every internal system must defend itself, every lateral path must be gated, and every credential must be treated as stealable. The practical consequences for an endpoint operator are concrete. First, blast radius: assume any single machine can be compromised, so design so that one compromised machine cannot become ten. That means workstation-to-workstation traffic is denied by default (you will build this in M06), local admin is removed (M04), and data cannot walk out on a USB stick (M05). Second, no implicit trust between services: the accounting app server does not trust requests just because they arrive from the office subnet; each request is authenticated and authorized. Third, continuous diagnostics and mitigation: you do not audit quarterly and hope; you monitor the enforcement points continuously and treat every blocked action as a signal (that signal pipeline is M07). Worked example: two designs for a 200-seat company. Design A trusts the LAN: flat network, local admins everywhere, file shares open to 'Authenticated Users.' One phished credential gives the attacker the workstation, the admin hash gives them the domain, the open shares give them the data. Mean time from one click to domain-wide ransomware: hours. Design B assumes breach: workstations cannot talk to each other, no local admins, applications allowlisted and ringfenced, USB blocked, egress filtered. The same phished credential yields one isolated workstation whose malicious child processes are blocked at launch, whose lateral movement hits closed ports, and whose exfiltration hits closed egress. The attacker still got in — assume breach concedes that — but the breach stays a single-machine event instead of a company event. The operator gotcha is treating assume breach as a slogan on a slide. It is a test you run against every design: 'if this machine is already owned, what can the attacker reach from here?' If the answer is 'everything,' you do not have zero trust yet; you have a perimeter with extra steps. Make that question a habit and you will naturally produce the policies this course teaches you to build.  One more operational habit: test your assume-breach posture with tabletop exercises, not just architecture diagrams. Pick a scenario — 'the CFO's laptop is compromised right now' — and walk the team through what the attacker can reach from that machine in the first hour. If the honest answer includes the file server, the backup system, or the domain controller, the design has gaps regardless of what the slide deck claims. Run this exercise quarterly; the gaps it finds become the next quarter's policy projects, which is how assume breach turns from a mindset into a roadmap.
notes.title: Assume breach: the mindset that makes the architecture work

notes.body: In the NIST model the PEP is abstract — it can be a gateway, a proxy, an agent. On the endpoint, the application-control agent is the PEP for the most fundamental question a machine can be asked: may this code execute? Everything else the platform does hangs off that gate. Allowlisting (Application Control) is deny-by-default execution: when a process launch is requested, the agent checks identity — hash, certificate, path — against policy and permits only what is explicitly allowed. Ringfencing then constrains what the allowed application may do once running: which child processes it may spawn, whether it may touch the registry, which files it may read or write, which network connections it may open. Elevation Control decides whether the application may run with administrative rights, removing standing local admin and granting just-in-time elevation per policy. Storage Control and Network Control extend the same deny-by-default logic to data paths and network paths. Detect turns every block into an alert, and Configuration Manager keeps the underlying Defender baseline from drifting. See the pattern: each module takes one abuse path and flips it from default-allow to default-deny. The operator insight is that these modules are not seven separate products; they are one policy engine applied to seven questions: may it run, what may it do, with what privilege, where may data go, where may packets go, what was blocked, and is the baseline intact? Worked example: map a single attack chain to the gates. Phishing email delivers a malicious document. Gate 1 (allowlisting): the document's embedded payload tries to drop an unknown executable — blocked, not on the allowlist. Suppose instead the payload is a malicious macro inside an allowed Office app — it passes gate 1 because Word itself is allowed. Gate 2 (ringfencing): the macro tries to spawn PowerShell — Word's ringfence denies child process creation. Suppose the macro instead tries to write to a startup folder — gate 2 denies the file write. Suppose the attacker pivots to credential theft — gate 3 (elevation): no local admin, no privileged foothold. Exfiltration over USB — gate 4 (storage): device blocked. Callback to attacker infrastructure — gate 5 (network): egress denied for the unapproved process. Every step of the kill chain meets a default-deny gate, and each block emits a Detect alert. Common gotcha: presenting the modules as overlapping or redundant. They are layered: each assumes the previous layer can be bypassed and catches what falls through. That is defense in depth expressed as policy, and it is the answer when the panel asks 'isn't allowlisting enough?'
notes.title: The endpoint as enforcement point: how allowlisting fits the model

notes.body: Let us trace the same attack against two endpoints, minute by minute, and watch where each model breaks. The scenario: at 9:02 AM, an accountant opens what looks like a vendor invoice. The document contains a malicious macro. This is a generic pattern — no exotic zero-day, just the commodity attack chain that encrypts companies every week. Against the default-allow endpoint: 9:02:14, the macro executes because Office macros are permitted and nothing evaluates the payload. 9:02:31, the macro drops invoice_helper.exe into the user's temp folder and launches it — no gate checks whether this binary is known-good. 9:03:05, the binary disables shadow copies and begins enumerating network shares; the endpoint firewall allows outbound SMB to neighbors because workstation-to-workstation traffic was never restricted. 9:04:40, it contacts its command server over HTTPS — egress is default-allow, so the callback succeeds. 9:06:12, encryption begins on local files and mapped shares. 9:07:00, the antivirus finally flags the binary by signature — forty-five seconds after the damage started, and the signature only exists because someone else was hit first. Total defender actions before detonation: zero. The model required the threat to be known, and it was not known in time. Against the default-deny endpoint: 9:02:14, the macro attempts to spawn a child process — the Office application's ringfence policy denies child process creation for winword.exe, and the attempt is logged. 9:02:15, the macro's fallback tries to write an executable to the temp folder — the ringfence denies the file write outside approved paths. 9:02:16, suppose the attacker anticipated this and the payload instead arrives as a standalone executable the user is tricked into running: the allowlisting PEP checks the binary's hash and certificate against policy — unknown, so execution is denied before a single instruction runs. 9:02:17, Detect fires an alert: blocked child-process spawn from winword.exe on ACCOUNTING-07. The SOC now has a lead at the attempt stage, not the encryption stage. 9:03:00, even if every application-layer gate somehow failed, the endpoint firewall's default-deny inbound rules block the SMB enumeration of neighbors, and egress filtering blocks the unknown binary's callback. The attack dies at the first gate it meets, and there are five gates. The teaching point is not that default-deny is magic — a sufficiently privileged, signed, allowed application abused in a permitted way can still cause harm, which is why the layers overlap. The point is the shift in who needs to be perfect: default-allow needs the defender to recognize every novel threat before it acts; default-deny needs the attacker to be running explicitly approved code behaving within its fence. Study this trace until you can whiteboard it. The panel will very likely ask some version of 'walk me through what happens when ransomware hits a protected endpoint,' and this minute-by-minute telling — attempt, block, alert, containment — is the answer that shows operator thinking instead of marketing recall.
notes.title: Worked example: ransomware detonation, default-allow vs default-deny

notes.body: Here is the truth that separates operators from tool buyers: in a deny-by-default world, the policy is the product. The agent is just the enforcement mechanism; the value — and the risk — lives in the rules you write, the approvals you grant, and the exceptions you allow to rot. A sloppy allowlist with a standing 'allow everything from the downloads folder' exception is default-allow wearing a default-deny costume. So the operational discipline has four parts. First, policy authorship: every rule needs an owner, a business justification, a scope (which users, which machines, which groups), and an expiry or review date. 'Allow chrome.exe' is not a rule; 'Allow Google Chrome stable, publisher Google LLC, for the Sales group, reviewed quarterly' is a rule. Second, change management: application updates change hashes, so your policy must handle trusted updaters — the vendor's own update mechanism — or every Patch Tuesday becomes a company-wide outage. You will design updater rules in M02; internalize now that update handling is the number-one operational burden of allowlisting and the number-one place junior operators get burned. Third, the approval workflow: when a user hits a block on legitimate software, the path from block to approval must be measured in minutes or hours, not days. A slow approval process teaches users that security is the department of 'no,' and they will find workarounds — personal devices, shadow IT — that are worse than the risk you were managing. Fourth, exception hygiene: every temporary exception ('allow this unsigned installer for the migration weekend') gets a ticket, an owner, and an automatic expiry. Review the exception list monthly; exceptions that outlive their justification become permanent holes. Worked example: the accounting office needs a new payroll app. The operator verifies the publisher certificate, checks the vendor's published hash, scopes the rule to the accounting group, sets a 90-day review, and documents the business justification in the ticket. The app updates itself monthly via its own updater — so the operator adds a trusted-updater rule for the vendor's signed updater rather than re-approving every version. When the panel asks 'how do you keep allowlisting from breaking the business,' this is the answer: updater rules for the churn, a fast approval lane for the new, scoped rules with reviews for everything, and exceptions that expire. Common gotcha: writing policy for the lab and forgetting policy for the humans. The workflow around the policy — who approves, how fast, what evidence — matters as much as the rules themselves.
notes.title: Policy as the product: the operational discipline

handsOnLab.brief: You will build a complete allowlist policy plan for a fictional 25-seat accounting office: application inventory by role, identity strategy per app (hash vs certificate vs updater rule), the approval workflow with SLAs, and the exception register. This is the exact artifact a junior operator would be asked to draft in week one.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every app in the inventory has an identity strategy and a scope; the approval workflow names approvers and SLAs; the exception register has no permanent blanket exceptions.
handsOnLab.deliverable: allowlist-plan.md — inventory table, rule set, approval workflow, updater strategy, and exception register for the 25-seat office.
steps: Define the office: 25 seats across 3 roles — 15 accountants, 5 payroll/HR, 5 managers. List every application each role needs (OS, Office suite, PDF reader, browser, accounting package, payroll tool, AV/EDR agent, printer drivers, remote support tool).
For each application, record the publisher and whether it is signed. Mark unsigned or unknown-publisher items for special handling.
Choose the identity strategy per app: certificate rule for signed software from reputable publishers, hash rule for unsigned legacy tools, and flag which apps have auto-updaters.
Design the trusted-updater rules: for each auto-updating app, write the rule that allows the vendor's signed updater to replace files it owns — name the updater binary and its publisher.

Write the approval workflow: who can request (any user via ticket), who approves (IT lead for standard apps, security lead for unsigned/unknown), evidence required (publisher verification, vendor hash check), and SLAs (4 business hours standard, 1 hour emergency lane with post-hoc review).

Draft the unknown-file handling procedure: quarantine, independent publisher verification, reputation check, sandbox detonation concept for high-risk files, and the deny-by-default verdict when verification fails.

Create the exception register template with columns: exception, scope, owner, justification, expiry date, review date — and enter two realistic examples (migration-weekend installer, legacy plant-floor tool) with expiries, not permanent entries.

Write the monitor-to-secured rollout plan: 30 days of monitor mode covering a full month-end close, weekly reviews of the unknown list, then a staged flip to Secured by department with a rollback criterion.
Add the allowlist hygiene schedule: quarterly stale-rule review, leaver-process approval cleanup, and the rule against blanket path exceptions.
Read the finished plan as the approver: confirm no rule says 'allow everything in <folder>' and every unsigned app has a compensating control.

notes.body: Application allowlisting lives or dies on its rollout, and the rollout has two modes you must never confuse. Monitor mode (sometimes called learning mode) observes: when an unknown binary executes, the agent logs the attempt — hash, path, parent process, user — but lets it run. Secured mode enforces: the same attempt is blocked. The safe path is always monitor first, secured second, and the reason is operational, not technical. On day one you do not know what the business actually runs. There are month-end close tools, quarterly tax utilities, the plant-floor label printer driver from 2014, and the manager's favorite PDF merger. Flip straight to Secured and you will block the payroll run on the 30th and spend the next week being hated. Monitor mode buys you the inventory: a complete, real-world list of what executes, built from observation instead of interviews (users always forget half their tools). Worked example: a 60-seat rollout. Weeks 1-4 run monitor mode, covering a full month-end close so the accounting batch jobs appear. Each Friday the operator reviews the unknown list: approves the legitimate (tax software update, new hire's scanner driver), investigates the suspicious (unsigned downloader in temp), and builds rules. By week 5 the unknown list is short and classified. Then the flip: Secured mode, but staged — pilot group first, then departments, with a rollback criterion ('if legitimate blocks exceed 5 per day in the pilot, we pause and review'). The emergency lane matters here: on flip day, a same-day approval path for anything wrongly blocked. Common gotcha: running monitor mode forever. Monitor mode is a phase, not a posture — an agent that only logs is a very expensive notepad. Set the flip date before you start monitoring, and treat 'we are still learning' after 60 days as a failure to decide. Second gotcha: monitoring too short a window. Two weeks misses the monthly jobs; monitor through at least one full business cycle. When the panel asks about your rollout experience, this staged story — monitor, classify, updater rules, staged enforcement — is what operator-grade sounds like.  The rollback criterion deserves the same rigor as the flip criteria. Define it before you start: for example, 'if legitimate blocks exceed five per user per day in the pilot group for two consecutive days, we return the pilot to monitor mode and review.' A rollback plan you write during the crisis is not a plan. Also decide who can authorize the flip in each direction — the same person who owns the policy — so enforcement decisions never stall waiting for a committee. Staged rollouts with written forward and reverse criteria are what separate a controlled deployment from an outage with good intentions.
notes.title: Learning Mode vs Secured: the only safe rollout order

notes.body: An allowlist is a list of identities, so the entire control reduces to one question: how do you identify a file reliably? There are three answers, each with a failure mode you must know. Hash identity (SHA-256 of the file bytes) is precise: it identifies exactly this version of this file, and any one-byte change — including a trojaned update — breaks the match and fails closed. The cost is churn: every vendor update changes the hash, so without updater rules you re-approve the world monthly. Certificate identity trusts the publisher: any binary signed by the vendor's code-signing certificate is allowed, which survives updates beautifully. The failure modes are real: a stolen vendor certificate lets malware ride the trust (this has happened to real vendors), and a legitimate-but-risky publisher gets a free pass for everything they sign. Path identity ('allow everything in C:\Program Files\Vendor\') is the weakest: it is cheap to write and trivially abused — malware simply lands in the allowed folder. Worked example: approving Google Chrome. The hash approach means re-approving every six-week release. The certificate approach — publisher Google LLC — auto-allows updates but also allows any other Google-signed binary. The path approach — allow C:\Program Files\Google\Chrome\* — lets an attacker drop evil.exe into that folder. The operator-grade answer is layered: certificate rule for the publisher plus a trusted-updater rule for the vendor's signed updater binary, with the updater constrained to replacing files the vendor owns. For unsigned legacy tools where no certificate exists, hash-pinning the specific approved version is the honest choice — precise, with documented churn cost. Common gotcha: certificate rules that are too broad. 'Allow anything signed by Microsoft' is effectively default-allow for the most-abused publisher on earth — scope certificate rules to the product or use them only for vendors with a clean, narrow signing practice. Second gotcha: forgetting that signatures can be valid but the file still malicious — a signed binary from a compromised vendor is allowed by your rule, which is why ringfencing (M03) constrains what allowed apps may do. Identity gets the app through the gate; behavior rules watch it inside.  In practice you verify signatures with the platform's own tooling: on Windows, Get-AuthenticodeSignature shows the signer and the chain status, and a Valid result means the signature is intact and chains to a trusted root — it does not mean the file is safe. Build the habit of checking the chain, not just the presence of a signature: a Valid signature from an unknown publisher is a fact to investigate, while a HashMismatch or NotSigned result on a file that claims to be vendor software is a finding. Record the signer subject and the thumbprint in your rule documentation so future-you can tell whether the vendor rotated their certificate or something changed unexpectedly.
notes.title: File identity: hash, certificate, and path

notes.body: No operator hand-writes rules for every copy of Chrome on earth, which is why allowlisting platforms ship a built-in applications library: a curated catalog of known-good applications with pre-built rules. Think of it as the shared starting inventory — common business software already identified by hash sets or publisher certificates, ready to be approved into your policy with a click instead of a forensic exercise. The value is speed: on day one you can approve the standard stack (office suites, browsers, PDF readers, common utilities) from the library instead of discovering each binary the hard way. But the library is a starting point, not a verdict, and treating it as one is the classic junior mistake. Three cautions. First, the library knows common software, not your software: the accounting package, the plant-floor tools, the custom line-of-business app — those are yours to identify and rule. Second, library entries are someone else's judgment about what is safe; your policy still needs your scoping (which groups, which machines) and your review cadence. A library rule that allows a remote-access tool globally because 'it is a known application' is a policy failure, not a library failure. Third, libraries age: vendors change publishers, products get acquired, signing certificates rotate. Your change process must catch the drift. Worked example: rolling out to the accounting office from the lab. The library covers the office suite, the browser, the PDF reader, and the OS utilities — approve those in bulk with group scoping. The accounting package and the payroll tool are not in the library: for those you collect the installer, verify the publisher certificate against the vendor's published documentation, hash the approved version, and write your own rules with a review date. The unknown list from monitor mode then tells you what you missed: the scanner driver, the label printer software, the manager's PDF tool. Each gets the same treatment: verify, rule, scope, review date. Common gotcha: approving library entries without scoping. 'Allow TeamViewer (known app)' for the whole company because the library says it is legitimate is how you authorize shadow remote access. The library tells you what the software is; you decide who may run it.  Treat the library as a supply chain: ask who curates it, how often it updates, and what happens when a listed application is found to be compromised. Your change process should include a periodic review of library-sourced rules — quarterly is the working default — where you confirm the entries you depend on are still current and still scoped correctly. If the platform ever flags a library entry as revoked or untrusted, you need a runbook entry for that day: which of your rules referenced it, what breaks if you pull it, and what the replacement rule looks like. Depending on a shared catalog without a plan for its failure modes is outsourcing judgment without retaining oversight.
notes.title: The built-in applications library: shared starting inventory

notes.body: Every block of legitimate software is a ticket, and the workflow that handles those tickets determines whether allowlisting survives contact with the business. A good approval workflow has five parts. Intake: a single channel (service desk ticket, portal request) that captures who, what, why, and the file itself or its hash — 'please allow the thing' is not an intake. Verification: the operator confirms what the software actually is — publisher certificate checked, vendor hash compared against the vendor's published value, reputation checked — through channels independent of the requester. Never verify software using the download link the user provides; fetch the vendor's published hash yourself. Decision: approve, approve-with-conditions (scoped, time-bound), or deny, made by someone with the authority and the knowledge — standard business apps by the IT lead, unsigned or unknown-publisher software by the security lead. Implementation: the rule is written with full shape — identity, scope (users/groups/machines), justification, review date — not a bare filename. Communication: the requester is told what was decided and why, because a denied user who understands the reason files better requests next time. Worked example: a designer requests a new video converter. Intake captures the vendor name and the installer hash. Verification: the operator downloads the vendor's published checksum, confirms the hash matches, checks the code signature, and finds the vendor is legitimate but the product bundles an optional adware component. Decision: approve with conditions — allow the application, ringfence it against network access it does not need, scope to the design group, 90-day review. Implementation and communication follow. The SLA is the load-bearing wall: standard requests in four business hours, emergency lane in one hour with post-hoc review. Miss the SLA repeatedly and users learn that security is the department of no — then comes shadow IT. Common gotcha: approvals without expiry on exceptions. 'Temporary' approvals that never expire are permanent rules that skipped the review. Every exception gets an owner and an expiry; the calendar, not someone's memory, enforces the review. Second gotcha: approver shopping — users re-submitting denied requests to a friendlier approver. One intake, one decision record, denials documented with reasons.  Measure the workflow or it will decay. Track three numbers weekly: median time from block to decision, the age of the oldest open request, and the approval rate by category. A median that creeps upward means the approvers are overloaded or the intake is capturing junk — either way, the business is learning that requests go nowhere. Publish the numbers to the approvers themselves; nothing fixes a slow queue like its owner seeing it in a chart. And keep an emergency lane genuinely fast: if the emergency path takes as long as the standard path, users will stop distinguishing them and every request will arrive marked urgent.
notes.title: Application approval workflows that the business can live with

notes.body: The unknown file is the moment of truth for default-deny: a binary with no rule, no library entry, and no reputation. The workflow must be fast, evidence-driven, and default to no. Step one is containment without drama: the file is blocked from executing, and a copy is preserved for analysis — you do not delete evidence you have not examined. Step two is identification: hash it, check the signature status, extract the publisher if signed, note the parent process and the delivery vector (email attachment, USB, download). Step three is independent verification: look up the hash in reputation sources, check the vendor's published hashes, and confirm the publisher through the vendor's own site — not through any link bundled with the file. Step four is the verdict, and there are only three: approve (verified legitimate, business-needed — write the full rule), approve-with-conditions (legitimate but risky — scoped, ringfenced, time-bound), or deny (unverifiable, unnecessary, or malicious — document the reason and, if malicious, escalate to incident response). Worked example: helpdesk receives 'invoice_scan.exe,' unsigned, delivered via email, hash unknown to reputation sources, and the 'vendor' has no website. Verdict: deny. The requester is told why in plain language, the file is retained per the incident process, and the ticket records the decision. Contrast: 'labelprint_driver.exe,' unsigned, needed for the warehouse printers, vendor is a real industrial company with a support line — the operator calls the vendor, confirms the published hash matches, and approves with a hash-pinned rule scoped to the warehouse machines, 90-day review, plus a note to revisit when the vendor starts signing. Common gotcha: treating 'my manager said it's fine' as verification. Authority is not evidence; the manager's approval authorizes the business need, but the file still gets the technical verification. Second gotcha: detonating unknown files on production machines 'just to see.' Unknown binaries are examined in isolated conditions or not at all — curiosity on a production endpoint is how incidents start. The discipline to internalize: every unknown file gets the same four steps, every time, because the one you skip is the one that matters.  For high-risk files, the examination happens under isolated conditions: a disposable virtual machine with no network access to production, snapshots so you can revert, and no credentials or sensitive data present. What you are looking for is behavior, not just identity — what the file tries to do when executed — and you record the observations in the ticket before deleting the VM. Never reuse the analysis VM for anything else, and never move the file to production 'because it looked fine in the sandbox.' The sandbox informs the verdict; the verdict still goes through the approval workflow with its evidence attached.
notes.title: Handling unknown files: the four-step verdict

notes.body: Allowing an application to run says nothing about what it may launch, and attackers live in that gap. Parent-child process rules close it: every process creation is evaluated independently, so the parent's approval never transfers to the child. This is where allowlisting meets ringfencing, and you need both halves of the story. The allowlisting half: when winword.exe spawns powershell.exe, the agent checks powershell.exe against policy on its own merits. If PowerShell is not approved for the accounting group, the child is blocked even though the parent is allowed. The ringfencing half (full depth in M03): even when the child is an allowed application, the parent's ringfence policy can forbid the spawn — Word is simply not permitted to create child processes, period. Worked example, the invoice macro attack from M01: the macro instructs Word to launch a payload. Layer one: the payload binary is unknown, so allowlisting blocks the child at spawn — verdict: denied, not on the allowlist. Suppose instead the macro launches powershell.exe, which is a legitimate Windows binary. Layer two: PowerShell is allowlisted for the IT group but not for accounting, so the child is blocked by group scope. Suppose the attacker targets an IT workstation where PowerShell is allowed: layer three, the ringfence — Word's policy denies child process creation regardless of the child's identity, so the spawn is blocked and logged. Three independent evaluations, any one of which stops the chain. The operator's job is designing these rules deliberately: which applications may spawn children at all, and which children may they spawn? Browsers spawn renderers and updaters — expected. Word spawning cmd.exe — never expected. Common gotcha: the 'trusted parent' shortcut. 'Allow everything launched by our management agent' feels efficient and creates a single bypass for the entire policy — compromise the agent, inherit its trust. Children are evaluated on their own identity, always. Second gotcha: forgetting script interpreters. Blocking powershell.exe while allowing wscript.exe, mshta.exe, and rundll32.exe leaves the same capability under different names — child-process policy must cover the interpreter family, which is exactly the ringfencing design work you will do in M03.  Extend the same thinking beyond direct child processes. Scheduled tasks, services, WMI event subscriptions, and startup-folder entries are all ways to get code running without an obvious parent-child relationship — the persistence layer. Your policy should treat these as execution events subject to the same identity checks: a scheduled task launching an unknown binary is the same verdict as a user double-clicking it. When you audit an endpoint, enumerate these autostart locations alongside the running processes; attackers who cannot win the parent-child game will play the persistence game instead, and the allowlist must cover both boards.

notes.body: Ringfencing starts from an uncomfortable truth: allowlisting answers 'may this code run?' but says nothing about what the code may do once running. A trusted application is not a safe application — it is an application whose behavior you have not constrained yet. Ringfencing constrains it. For each allowed application, policy defines four behavior boundaries: which other applications or processes it may execute (child-process control), whether it may edit the registry and which keys, which files it may read and write and where, and which network sessions it may open. Anything outside the fence is denied and logged. The mental model is a playpen: the app is welcome inside, but the walls are real. Consider why this matters operationally. The most common endpoint attacks do not begin with an unknown binary — they begin with a trusted one. A Word document with a malicious macro, a browser exploit, a signed administrative tool turned against its owner: in every case the parent application is legitimate, allowed, and doing something it was never supposed to do. Allowlisting waves the parent through; ringfencing stops the abuse. Worked example: compare two policies for winword.exe. Policy A (allowlist only): Word may run. A macro instructs Word to launch powershell.exe with an encoded command — Word is allowed, PowerShell is a signed Windows binary, nothing stops the chain. Policy B (allowlist plus ringfence): Word may run, but its fence denies child-process creation, denies writes outside the user's document folders, denies registry edits, and denies network sessions. The same macro now fails four independent ways: the spawn is blocked, the payload write is blocked, the persistence registry key is blocked, and the callback is blocked. Each block is logged with full context — parent, attempted action, target — which becomes the alert feed you will triage in M07. Common gotcha: thinking of ringfencing as 'extra allowlisting.' It is a different question entirely. Allowlisting is identity (is this code approved?); ringfencing is behavior (is this action permitted for this app?). You need both because attackers defeat identity controls by borrowing trusted identities. Second gotcha: fencing everything identically. A browser legitimately needs network access; a PDF reader does not. The fence follows the application's legitimate function — least privilege applied per application, not per machine.  A subtle point: fences should inherit down the process tree. When a fenced application legitimately spawns an approved child — the browser's renderer, the updater — that child should run under a fence at least as strict as the parent's, not escape into an unfenced context. Otherwise the attacker only needs to compromise the allowed child to inherit its freedom. Define the expected child family per application explicitly, fence each member for its own function, and deny everything outside the family. The process tree is the unit of policy, not just the single process.
notes.title: What ringfencing is: behavior control for allowed apps

notes.body: The canonical ringfence-bypass pattern — the one you must be able to whiteboard — is Word calling PowerShell. Walk it slowly. The attacker crafts a document containing a malicious macro. The user opens it in Word, which is allowlisted: the gate asks 'may Word run?' and the answer is yes. The macro executes inside Word's process and instructs the operating system to launch powershell.exe with a command that downloads and runs a payload. Under allowlisting alone, every binary in this chain is legitimate: Word is approved, PowerShell is a signed Microsoft binary. The attack succeeds without a single 'unknown' file. This is living-off-the-land: the attacker brings no tools, only instructions for your tools. The family has many members — script interpreters (powershell.exe, wscript.exe, cscript.exe), system utilities (rundll32.exe, mshta.exe, regsvr32.exe), and admin tools — all signed, all commonly allowed, all capable of executing attacker logic when invoked with the right arguments. Ringfencing breaks the pattern at the behavior layer. Word's fence states: this application may not create child processes. The macro's spawn request arrives, the fence evaluates the behavior (not the identity of PowerShell), and denies it. Note the elegance: the decision does not depend on recognizing powershell.exe as dangerous — it depends on Word having no legitimate need to spawn children. Worked example with numbers you can defend: in a 200-seat office, Word legitimately spawns child processes approximately never — its function is document editing. So a deny-child-processes fence for Word has a near-zero false-positive rate and blocks the entire macro-to-shell attack class. Contrast with a developer workstation where the IDE legitimately spawns compilers: there the fence must allow the compiler family and deny everything else, which is more work but the same principle. Common gotcha: blocking powershell.exe by identity while leaving wscript.exe, mshta.exe, and rundll32.exe allowed. The attacker simply switches interpreters — you blocked a name, not the capability. The ringfence must cover the interpreter family as behaviors: 'this app may not spawn script interpreters,' not 'this app may not spawn powershell.exe.' Second gotcha: forgetting that the fence must also cover the payload write and the persistence. Defense in depth means the macro fails at the spawn, and if it somehow writes a file, the file-write fence stops the drop, and if that fails, the registry fence stops the Run key. Layer the behaviors; never rely on one.  The deeper variant of this pattern does not even need a new binary: the attacker abuses the legitimate binary's own arguments. The same powershell.exe that your admins use becomes the payload delivery vehicle when invoked with an encoded command — identity checks see the trusted binary, and only behavior analysis sees the attack. This is why mature ringfence design constrains not just which children may spawn but what arguments the sensitive ones may carry: script interpreters launched with encoded or hidden-window arguments by a document reader are never legitimate. When you write the fence, think in terms of behaviors — 'this app may not invoke script interpreters at all' — rather than binary names, because the names are the attacker's to choose.
notes.title: The Word-calling-PowerShell pattern

notes.body: Some attacks do not even need a macro: they abuse the document handler chain itself. Consider the general class, taught here without vendor-specific exploit details: a specially crafted document, when merely previewed or opened, triggers an external protocol handler or helper application that the operating system launches automatically — and that helper, in turn, executes attacker-controlled commands. The user did not enable macros. The user did not click 'enable content.' The document format's own features did the work: the application that opened the document reached outside itself to invoke another program, and that program ran with the user's privileges. This class is why ringfencing covers more than child processes. A complete fence for a document reader constrains four behaviors against this pattern. First, child-process creation: the reader may not launch external handlers or helpers beyond its explicitly approved set. Second, the network session: even if a helper launches, it may not call out. Third, file writes: the helper may not drop payloads to disk. Fourth, registry edits: the helper may not establish persistence. Any one of these breaking the chain is sufficient; all four together make the class impractical. Worked example: design the fence for a PDF reader against handler-abuse. Child processes: deny all except the vendor's signed updater. Network: deny all — a reader's legitimate function (rendering documents) needs no network. File writes: allow only to the user's document folders; deny temp, startup, and system paths. Registry: deny all writes. Now walk the attack: the crafted PDF triggers a helper launch — blocked at child creation. Suppose the helper is somehow already present and invoked — its network call is blocked, its payload write is blocked, its persistence write is blocked. The document still renders for the legitimate user; the abuse class is fenced out. The operator lesson is about trust boundaries between applications: every time app A can invoke app B, that is a privilege boundary, and default-allow across it is the vulnerability. Ringfencing makes each such boundary default-deny. Common gotcha: assuming 'no macros' means 'no code execution.' Document formats are programs with rendering engines; the handler chain is the attack surface. Fence the behaviors, not just the macro setting.  Note that the preview pane counts as opening. Many document-abuse attacks trigger from the preview handler without the user ever double-clicking the file — the mere act of selecting the message renders the content through the vulnerable handler chain. Your user training should say 'do not preview unexpected attachments' rather than 'do not open them,' and your fence design should assume the handler runs on preview. This is also why the email gateway's attachment handling matters as a complementary layer: the fewer crafted documents that reach the inbox, the fewer handler invocations your fences must survive.
notes.title: Case study in general terms: when documents launch processes

notes.body: Browsers are the hardest applications to fence because their legitimate function is the attack surface: they download untrusted content, execute scripts, and open network connections by design. The fence cannot be 'deny everything' — it must be 'allow exactly the dangerous things the function requires, and nothing else.' Start with child processes. A modern browser legitimately spawns renderer processes, GPU processes, and its own updater — these are expected children, ideally constrained to the vendor's signed binaries. What it must never spawn is a command shell, a script interpreter, or an arbitrary downloaded executable. So the child-process fence is an allowlist within the fence: the renderer/updater family is permitted, everything else is denied. Next, file writes. The browser legitimately writes downloads to the user's download folder and cache to its profile. It must not write executables to startup folders, system directories, or temp paths that double as launch points — so the file-write fence permits user-content paths and denies execution-path writes. The download folder deserves special attention: it is the highest-risk directory on the machine, and the fence should ensure downloads there cannot be executed directly (that is the allowlist's job at launch, but the fence adds the write-side constraint). Network: the browser needs web access — that is its job — but the fence can still constrain it: deny connections to non-standard ports, deny raw socket behavior, and log aggressively. The updater is the delicate part: the browser must update itself, so the updater binary gets its own narrowly scoped permission to replace the browser's files — and only the browser's files. Worked example: an exploit compromises the renderer and attempts to spawn cmd.exe. The child-process fence denies the spawn — cmd.exe is not in the expected family — and logs the attempt with the renderer as parent. The exploit's fallback tries to write a payload to the startup folder — the file-write fence denies it. The fallback's fallback tries to open a raw connection to a non-standard port — the network fence denies it. Three behaviors, three denials, one alert bundle for triage. Common gotcha: fencing the browser so tightly that updates break. A browser that cannot update becomes the vulnerability — the updater carve-out is not a weakness in the fence, it is load-bearing. Second gotcha: forgetting extensions and plugins as child-equivalents. The fence should account for what the browser is permitted to load, not just what it may spawn.
notes.title: Ringfence design: browsers

notes.body: Office applications are the most attacked and the most fenceable: their legitimate function (editing documents, crunching spreadsheets, managing mail) requires almost none of the dangerous behaviors. The baseline Office fence is strict: deny child-process creation entirely — Word, Excel, and PowerPoint have no legitimate need to launch other programs. Deny registry writes except the vendor's own settings keys — Office does not need to register system services or set Run keys. Constrain file writes to user document locations — deny writes to startup folders, system directories, and temp-execution paths. Deny network sessions except explicitly approved collaboration endpoints and the updater — Word does not need arbitrary outbound connections. Outlook is the exception that proves the rule: it legitimately needs network access to mail servers, so its network fence is scoped to the mail protocols and servers the business uses, not the open internet. Now the honest complication: macros and add-ins. Businesses run on Excel macros — the finance team's month-end workbook is a program, and fencing it naively breaks the business. The operator-grade answer is not 'allow macros' (default-allow for code) but signed-macro policy: only macros signed by approved publishers execute, and even signed macros run inside the fence — they still cannot spawn children or write outside document paths. Worked example: the accounting team's month-end macro workbook. The workbook's macros are signed with the company's code-signing certificate. Policy: allow signed macros from the corporate publisher, and the Excel fence still denies child-process creation and non-document file writes. The macro calculates, formats, and saves — all permitted. An attacker who steals the workbook and adds a shell-spawning macro faces two gates: the signature check (their modification breaks the corporate signature) and the fence (the spawn is denied regardless). Common gotcha: the 'enable all macros for the finance team' exception. That is default-allow for the most macro-attacked applications in the company, scoped to the users with the most sensitive data. If the business truly needs unsigned macros, the compensating controls are a signed-macro migration plan with a date, plus tighter fences (no child processes, no network) on the machines that run them. Second gotcha: Outlook attachments. The fence constrains what Outlook may do, but the attachment the user saves and double-clicks is a new execution — that is the allowlist's gate (M02), and the two layers must be designed together.  Do not forget the browser's loadable code: extensions, plugins, and helper objects execute inside the browser's context with its privileges. A malicious or compromised extension bypasses the child-process fence entirely because it never spawns anything — it simply acts. Your browser policy should therefore govern the extension inventory too: an approved extension list, ideally centrally managed, with the same approval workflow as applications. An unmanaged extension ecosystem on a fenced browser is a fenced front door with the windows open.
notes.title: Ringfence design: Office applications

notes.body: PDF readers look harmless and are historically one of the most exploited application classes: complex parsers, JavaScript engines, and handler chains, all processing untrusted input. The fence for a PDF reader is the strictest of the three classes because the legitimate function is the narrowest: render documents. Child processes: deny entirely except the vendor's signed updater. A reader never legitimately launches other programs. Registry: deny all writes — a reader has no settings that require registry modification beyond its own keys, and persistence via the reader is never legitimate. File writes: allow only to user document folders for 'save as' functionality; deny temp, startup, and system paths absolutely. Network: deny entirely — rendering a document requires no network, and the updater gets its own narrow exception. This is the purest expression of least privilege per application: four denies and the app still does its job perfectly. Worked example: a crafted PDF attempts the handler-abuse pattern. It tries to invoke an external helper — child-process deny. It tries to execute embedded JavaScript that downloads a second stage — network deny. It tries to write the second stage to disk — file-write deny. It tries to register for persistence — registry deny. The user reads the invoice; the attack reads the fence. Now the validation discipline, because a fence you have not tested is a hope. Every ringfence policy gets a test plan before enforcement: for each deny, attempt the denied action with a harmless proof-of-concept on a test machine and confirm the block and the log. Attempt to spawn a child from the fenced app — confirm blocked and logged. Attempt the registry write — confirm blocked and logged. Attempt the file write to a denied path — confirm blocked and logged. Attempt the network session — confirm blocked and logged. Then attempt the legitimate workflows — open, edit, save, print, update — and confirm they work. Only then does the policy leave the pilot group. Common gotcha: testing only the blocks and not the legitimate workflows. A fence that blocks attacks and breaks work gets removed on Monday morning. Second gotcha: treating the PDF reader as 'not important' because it is not Word. Attackers do not share your ranking — they attack the reader precisely because defenders under-fence it. Fence it like it matters, because it does.  Two legacy Office features deserve explicit mention in your fence design: DDE and OLE. Both are mechanisms by which a document pulls in external content or launches linked objects — legitimate in 1998, abused ever since. If the business does not use them, disable them outright via policy rather than fencing around them; a disabled feature needs no fence. If some legacy workflow genuinely depends on them, that workflow gets the full treatment from M02: documented, scoped to the machines that need it, ringfenced tightly, with a migration plan and a date. 'Legacy requires it' is a bridge, not a destination.

notes.body: Local administrator rights are the single most consequential privilege on a Windows endpoint, and their removal is the single highest-leverage hardening step you can take. Understand why before you touch anything. An administrator can install software, modify system configuration, read other users' data, disable security tooling, and — critically — access credential material stored on the machine. When an attacker compromises a standard user, they get that user's files. When they compromise a local admin, they get the machine's credential store: hashes and tokens they can reuse to move laterally, often all the way to domain dominance. This is the pivot: local admin turns a single phished workstation into a stepping stone toward the entire environment. The statistics-free version of the argument is structural, not numerical: every privilege-escalation path, every credential-theft technique, and every persistence mechanism is easier, quieter, or only possible with administrative rights. Removing local admin does not make attacks impossible — it lowers every attack's ceiling and raises its noise. Worked example: two identical phishing compromises. On machine A the user is a local admin. The payload reads credential material from memory, reuses it against the file server, and within the hour the attacker holds a domain-level foothold. On machine B the user is standard. The payload runs in a low-privilege context: it cannot read the credential store, cannot install a driver-level persistence mechanism, cannot disable the agent. Its privilege-escalation attempts — the classic next step — hit the elevation policy and are denied and logged. The same initial click produces a contained single-machine event instead of an enterprise incident. The difference is entirely the standing privilege. Common gotcha: the 'but they need it' reflex. In practice, when organizations audit actual admin usage, the overwhelming majority of daily admin-rights usage is habit, not need: installing approved software (handled by software deployment), changing the clock (handled by policy), running a legacy tool once (handled by an elevation rule). The operator's job is to discover the real needs — which you do in monitor mode — and serve them with scoped elevation rather than standing privilege. Second gotcha: removing admin without the workflow. Take the privilege on Monday with no elevation path and by Wednesday the business has either revolted or routed around you. The removal and the just-in-time workflow ship together, always.  Before removing anything, measure. Pull 30 days of privilege-use data: which users invoke admin rights, for what operations, and how often. You will typically find three groups: the handful with genuine recurring needs (their tasks become elevation rules), the large middle whose 'need' is one legacy installer (their need becomes a scoped rule plus a remediation ticket), and the long tail who simply have admin because everyone does (their need evaporates on inspection). This data does two jobs: it designs the replacement policies, and it defuses the political fight — 'we measured, and here is what you actually use' beats 'trust us' in every meeting where admin removal is contested.
notes.title: Why local admin must go

notes.body: Just-in-time elevation is the replacement for standing admin: instead of the user holding administrative rights all day, the specific application or task is elevated for a scoped, time-bound need — then the privilege is gone. The user account itself never becomes an administrator. This distinction matters enormously. When you make someone a local admin, you grant a standing capability: every process they launch, every script they run, every piece of malware that lands in their session inherits administrative rights until someone remembers to remove them. When you elevate just the installer via policy, only that installer, launched for that task, holds the rights — the user's browser, email client, and everything else stay standard. The policy anatomy has five fields. Identity: which application may be elevated (publisher, hash, or path — the M02 identity discipline applies here too). Scope: which users or groups, on which machines. Conditions: when — business hours, ticket reference required, approval needed above a risk threshold. Duration: how long the elevation lasts — minutes for an installer, never permanent. Logging: every grant records who, what, why, when, and approved-by. Worked example: the monthly vendor driver update. Policy: 'VendorDriverSetup.exe, publisher Vendor Inc., may be elevated for the Helpdesk group on workstation OU, during business hours, with a ticket number, for 30 minutes, approved by the IT lead.' The technician runs the installer through the elevation workflow, it completes with admin rights, the window closes. The technician's account was standard before, during (outside that process), and after. Contrast with the old world: the technician is a local admin all month for a 10-minute task. Common gotcha: elevating the user 'temporarily' instead of the application. 'Temporary admin for the afternoon' is standing admin with a shorter memory — everything in the session inherits it, including the malware. Elevate the task, not the person. Second gotcha: elevation without conditions. An elevation rule with no ticket requirement, no time bound, and no approval is just admin rights with extra steps. The conditions are the control; write them tightly and review them quarterly.  Keep interactive elevation and non-interactive privilege strictly separated in your design. Services and scheduled tasks that run with stored credentials or as SYSTEM are not 'elevation' in the just-in-time sense — they are standing privilege by another name, and they get their own inventory, their own review, and their own hardening (managed service accounts, credential rotation, minimal rights). The just-in-time workflow covers the human asking for temporary rights; the service inventory covers the machine acting with permanent ones. Auditing one while ignoring the other leaves half the privilege surface unexamined.
notes.title: Just-in-time elevation: elevate the task, not the person

notes.body: Elevation policies are written per application, because different software has different legitimate needs and the policy must match the need — no more, no less. Start by categorizing the elevation requests you will actually see. Installers and updaters: the most common legitimate need. Policy: the vendor's signed installer may elevate, scoped to the machines that need the software, time-bound to the deployment window. Management agents: backup, patching, and monitoring tools that genuinely require system-level access. Policy: the agent's service binary is elevated by design (services run as SYSTEM), but its interactive components are not — scope carefully. Administrative utilities: disk tools, driver installers, network diagnostics. Policy: named tools for named groups (IT staff), with ticket requirements for the sensitive ones. Legacy line-of-business apps: the painful category — old software that demands admin for no good reason. Policy: explicit elevation rules as a bridge, paired with a remediation plan (vendor engagement, compatibility shims, or replacement) and a review date, because 'legacy needs admin' cannot be a permanent answer. Worked example: build the policy set for a 25-seat office. The PDF reader's updater: signed updater, may elevate, all workstations, automatic — no ticket needed, it is routine. The accounting package installer: signed installer, may elevate for the IT group only, during the quarterly update window, ticket required. The disk-imaging tool: IT group only, ticket required, 2-hour window, approved by the IT lead. The legacy label-printer driver (unsigned, demands admin): hash-pinned, warehouse machines only, ticket required, 90-day review, vendor contacted about a signed version. Four applications, four different policies, each matching the actual need. Common gotcha: one elevation policy for everything. 'IT staff may elevate anything' recreates standing admin for the highest-value targets — attackers specifically hunt IT credentials. Even IT gets per-application policies, with the sensitive ones requiring approval. Second gotcha: forgetting service accounts and scheduled tasks. Elevation policy covers interactive elevation; services and scheduled tasks with stored credentials are a separate inventory with their own review — a service running as SYSTEM with a weak password is admin rights by another name.  Verify before you elevate. An elevation policy that approves 'the vendor installer' should still confirm the installer's integrity at approval time: compare its hash against the vendor's published value, confirm the signature chains correctly, and confirm you fetched it from the vendor's official distribution point. Elevating a trojaned installer with administrative rights is the worst possible outcome of this control — the policy that grants the privilege must also demand the evidence. Build the verification step into the intake form so it cannot be skipped under time pressure: no hash check, no elevation.
notes.title: Elevation policies per application

notes.body: User Account Control is the prompt everyone loves to hate, and you need to understand exactly what it does and does not do before you layer policy over it. UAC has two prompt types. The consent prompt appears for administrators: 'Do you want to allow this app to make changes?' — a yes/no question to someone who already holds the rights. The credential prompt appears for standard users: 'Enter an administrator username and password' — a demand for credentials the user should not have. UAC's security value is real but narrow: it makes privilege use visible and gives malware one more click to socially engineer. Its weakness is structural: the decision is made by the user, at the moment, under time pressure — which is precisely when users click 'Yes' on whatever the urgent-looking installer demands. Malware has exploited this for years with fake installers that simply ask. Elevation Control moves the decision from the user to the policy. Under policy-driven elevation, the user does not get a yes/no prompt to adjudicate — the agent consults policy: is this application approved for elevation, for this user, under these conditions? If yes, it elevates with full logging. If no, it denies with full logging. The user experience actually improves: legitimate workflows elevate silently per policy instead of interrupting with prompts, while illegitimate ones are denied consistently rather than depending on the user's judgment at 4:55 PM on a Friday. Worked example: the standard-user accountant runs the approved payroll update. Old world: credential prompt, accountant calls helpdesk, helpdesk types the admin password (which the accountant shoulder-surfs), update runs. New world: the payroll updater matches the elevation policy (signed, IT-approved, ticket window), elevates without a prompt, logs the grant. Same outcome, no password shared, full audit trail. Now the attack case: malware drops a fake updater and triggers a UAC consent prompt on an admin's machine — the admin, busy, clicks Yes. Under elevation policy on a standard-user machine, there is no Yes to click: the binary is not in the elevation policy, so it is denied and logged. Common gotcha: thinking UAC 'is' the elevation control. UAC is a speed bump; policy-driven elevation is a gate. Keep UAC enabled (it still catches the unpolicied cases) but never rely on user judgment as the control. Second gotcha: 'quiet mode' UAC settings that auto-elevate. Any setting that removes the prompt without adding policy just removes the speed bump — verify UAC is at a sane level as part of the M08 Defender-plus-baseline work.
notes.title: UAC interplay: prompts are not policy

notes.body: Walk the stolen-credential scenario end to end, because this is the story the panel wants to hear and the threat the control defeats. The setup: a helpdesk technician with local admin on 200 workstations reuses a password. An attacker phishes the technician, harvests the credential, and now holds administrative rights on every machine the technician touched. Under standing admin, the attacker's next moves are textbook: authenticate to workstations with the stolen credential, read credential material from each newly owned machine, escalate toward domain admin, deploy ransomware enterprise-wide. The technician's single credential was a skeleton key because the privilege was standing, broad, and reusable. Now replay with Elevation Control deployed. The technician is a standard user. Their daily elevated tasks — running the approved installer, the driver update — were performed through just-in-time elevation: the task elevated, the account did not. The phished credential is a standard-user credential: it authenticates, but it grants no administrative rights anywhere. The attacker's lateral movement attempts hit closed doors: no admin shares to plunder, no credential store readable, no remote admin tools permitted by Network Control policy. To escalate, the attacker must now defeat the elevation policy itself — requesting elevation for an unapproved binary, which is denied and logged, generating the Detect alert that starts the incident response at the attempt stage. The blast radius collapses from 'the enterprise' to 'one standard-user session.' Worked example with the workflow: the attacker, holding the phished standard credential, submits an elevation request for their payload through the helpdesk channel (the only path). Identity verification fails — the requester cannot prove they are the technician under duress procedures — and even a social-engineered approval would only elevate the named application for a time-bound window, not the attacker's session. Every step is logged. Common gotcha: believing elevation control replaces credential hygiene. It does not — the phished credential still grants the user's data and email. What it does is cap the damage: credential theft without standing privilege is a contained incident, not an enterprise one. Pair it with phishing-resistant authentication and the attacker's path narrows to nearly nothing. Second gotcha: the break-glass account. You will keep one sealed emergency admin credential — and its use must fire an immediate alert, because in a no-standing-admin world, any use of it is an exceptional event worth waking someone for.  Assume the attacker also steals session tokens, not just passwords — tokens can be replayed without the password ever being known. This is why the control pairs with session hygiene: short token lifetimes, and elevation decisions that re-verify rather than trusting an existing session blindly. The principle is the same as everywhere in this course: standing artifacts — passwords, tokens, privileges — are what attackers reuse. Shrink what stands, time-bound what is granted, and log every grant so the reuse window is visible.
notes.title: The stolen-credential pivot scenario

notes.body: The helpdesk elevation workflow is where policy meets humans, and its design decides whether the control survives. It has five steps, each non-optional. Intake: the requester submits who they are, what application needs elevation, the business reason, the ticket number, and the time window. 'Need admin plz' is not an intake — the form enforces the evidence. Identity verification: the helpdesk verifies the requester is who they claim — callback to the known number, in-person for sensitive requests, never trust the request channel alone (the 'urgent admin request' email from the 'CFO' is a classic social-engineering lure). Scoped approval: the approver checks the application against policy — is this app approved for elevation for this user? If yes and routine, approve; if sensitive or unprecedented, escalate to the security lead. The approval names the application, the machine, and the window — never 'admin for the afternoon.' Execution with logging: the elevation is granted through the agent, and the grant is logged with who, what, why, window, and approver. Post-hoc review: a sample of grants is reviewed weekly — was the business reason real, did the window match the need, any anomalies? Worked example: Tuesday 10 AM, a designer needs to install a font management tool. Intake: designer, FontTool Setup 4.2, vendor-signed, ticket HD-4821, today 10-12. Verification: helpdesk calls the designer's known extension. Approval: the tool is on the approved-elevation list for the design group — approved, 2-hour window, this machine. Execution: the installer elevates, completes, window closes. Review: Friday's sample includes HD-4821 — business reason confirmed, window matched. Total friction: one form and one callback. The emergency lane handles the 2 AM server case: on-call approver, same evidence, mandatory next-business-day review — emergencies get speed, not exemption. Common gotcha: verification theater. 'We verified identity' by replying to the same email thread that made the request proves nothing. Verify through an independent channel, every time, especially for sensitive elevations. Second gotcha: approval without expiry. An approved elevation that stays open 'until the work is done' is standing admin with paperwork. The window closes automatically; a new window needs a new approval.  Design the emergency lane with the same care as the standard path, because emergencies are when discipline is weakest. The lane needs three things: a reachable approver (the on-call rotation, not 'whoever is awake'), the same evidence minimum (ticket number, application identity, window — no evidence-free elevations, ever), and a mandatory next-business-day review where the grant is re-examined with cool heads. Publish the lane's usage statistics monthly: a lane used twice a quarter is healthy; a lane used twice a week is a standard path avoiding scrutiny, and the review will show it.
