notes.body: Storage Control applies deny-by-default to the question every exfiltration attempt asks: can data move through this path? The module governs three things: storage devices (what may connect to the endpoint), file paths (where data may be written), and shares (who may read or write network storage). The device side is the most visible: USB mass storage sticks, external hard drives, phones and tablets connecting over MTP/PTP, optical media, and Bluetooth file transfer each get a policy — typically deny or read-only by default, with narrowly scoped exceptions. The path side constrains where even allowed writes may land: sensitive directories can be sealed against writes from removable sources, and application data folders can be fenced off from user-level copying. The share side extends the same logic to the network: file shares default to read-only, with read-write granted per group, per share, with justification. The unifying principle is that data movement is a privileged action, not a background capability. In the default-allow world, any process running as the user can copy any file the user can read to any device the OS recognizes — which is why the 'customer database on a USB stick' scenario is a one-line copy command. In the default-deny world, the copy hits the device policy before the first byte moves. Worked example: the Friday-afternoon insider. An employee decides to take the client list. They plug in a personal USB stick. The device class (USB mass storage) is deny-write by default for their group. The copy command fails; the attempt is logged with device ID, user, timestamp, and the file paths touched. The employee tries their phone instead — MTP storage class, same deny. They try uploading to personal cloud storage — the network egress policy (M06) denies the unapproved destination. Three paths, three denials, one alert bundle. The data never moved. Common gotcha: scoping device policy by machine instead of by user-and-machine. A 'blocked' USB stick that works when moved to another workstation is not a control; it is a suggestion. Policy must follow the device class and the user so the denial is consistent everywhere. Second gotcha: forgetting the read direction. Blocking writes stops exfiltration, but allowing reads from untrusted media invites malware in — the full policy addresses both directions, and the incident walkthrough later in this module assumes you have the logs for both.  Cover the read direction with equal seriousness. Blocking writes stops exfiltration, but unrestricted reads from untrusted media invite malware in — the stick found in the parking lot is the classic delivery vector. The complete device policy states both directions per class: the field tech's registered drive may read and write, the conference-room PC may read presentation drives but never write to them, and unknown media is denied both directions. When you write the policy table, give every class two columns — read and write — and force an explicit decision in each. Blank cells become holes.
notes.title: What Storage Control governs: devices, paths, shares

notes.body: Device policy lives or dies on its class coverage, because attackers and careless users alike route around the classes you forgot. USB mass storage is the obvious one — the classic stick — and the default posture is deny-write, with read-only or full deny as the stricter variants. But the stick is only the beginning. Phones and tablets connecting over USB present themselves as MTP or PTP storage devices: to the OS they are storage, and 'I was just charging it' is not a policy exception — if it mounts as storage, the storage policy applies. External hard drives and SSDs are USB mass storage with more capacity and the same policy. Optical media (DVD-RW) still exists in some environments and gets its own rule. Bluetooth file transfer and even some wireless presentation dongles move files without a cable — the policy must name them or they become the hole. For each class, the policy states the default (deny, read-only, or allow), the exception roles, the exception conditions, and the review date. Worked example: the 40-seat company device table. USB mass storage: default deny-write; exception: field technicians with company-registered encrypted drives. Phones/tablets (MTP/PTP): default deny — charging-only cables issued to remove the ambiguity. External HDDs: default deny; exception: IT backup role with registered drives. Optical: default deny; no exceptions (no business need found in the audit). Bluetooth file transfer: default deny; exception: none — presentation uses the approved wireless system. Five classes, five rows, zero unaddressed paths. The audit that produces this table is non-optional: you cannot write policy for device classes you have not inventoried, so the first step is always discovering what connects to your endpoints — asset management data, helpdesk tickets about 'my drive doesn't work,' and a monitor-mode observation period. Common gotcha: the 'charging' loophole. Users will insist the phone was just charging. Issue charging-only cables (no data pins) and the argument evaporates — engineering beats arguing. Second gotcha: personal vs company devices. The policy distinguishes them explicitly: company-registered encrypted drives for the exception roles, personal devices never — because you cannot verify encryption, ownership, or malware status on a personal stick, and 'just this once' is how the database leaves.  You cannot govern devices you have not discovered, so the policy project starts with an inventory. Pull from asset management, but verify: check the helpdesk ticket history for 'my drive doesn't work' and 'can't access my phone' (each ticket names a device class in use), run a monitor-mode observation period logging every storage-device connection with its class and user, and survey the departments with legitimate needs (field ops, sales, executives). The inventory will surprise you — the lab equipment with its ancient data logger, the marketing team's camera cards — and each surprise is a row in the policy table that would otherwise have been a hole.
notes.title: Device classes: the complete coverage problem

notes.body: Shares are storage too, and they get the same least-privilege treatment. The default posture for a network share is read-only for the groups that need it, with read-write granted narrowly, justified, and reviewed. Broad read-write shares are the insider's other favorite path: no USB stick required when the 'Finance' share lets every employee write — and the ransomware that encrypts mapped shares loves them too. Start with the inventory: every share, its purpose, its current permissions, and who actually uses it. Then apply the discipline: read access for the groups with a demonstrated need, write access only where the workflow requires it (the finance team writes to Finance; sales reads it), and no 'Everyone: Full Control' anywhere — that entry is a finding in every audit for a reason. Scoping follows the same per-user, per-group model as device policy: the policy engine evaluates the user and the machine, so the contractor on a loaner laptop gets different share access than the finance lead on their workstation. Worked example: the company's share redesign. Before: three shares, all 'Authenticated Users: Read/Write,' because it was easy in 2019. After: FINANCE — read for management and finance, write for finance only, reviewed quarterly. ENGINEERING — read for engineering and IT, write for engineering leads, reviewed quarterly. SHARED — read for all staff, write for department heads, with a 90-day review because shared folders accumulate sensitive data like sediment. The migration is staged: audit current usage first (who actually writes where — the logs will surprise you), announce the change, flip to the new permissions, and keep a two-week exception lane for the workflows you missed. The ransomware angle deserves emphasis: the M01 trace showed encryption spreading through mapped shares. Read-only-by-default shares do not just slow insiders; they contain the blast radius of a compromised standard user whose session can only read what the shares permit. Common gotcha: share permissions vs NTFS permissions confusion. Both layers must agree — a restrictive share with permissive NTFS (or vice versa) yields the permissive effective access. Document both, and verify effective access with a test account, not by reading the dialogs. Second gotcha: the 'temporary project share' that becomes permanent. Shares get owners and review dates like everything else in this course.  Remember that effective access is the intersection of both layers: the share permissions and the NTFS permissions must agree, or the more permissive one wins. Document both in the share record, and verify with a test account in each role — reading the dialogs is not verification. The classic failure is the 'secure' share with Everyone:Read at the share level and Users:Full at the NTFS level, or vice versa; the effective access is whatever the union permits. Your migration checklist should include an effective-access test per role per share, recorded in the ticket, before you declare the migration complete.
notes.title: Share permissions: least privilege on the network

notes.body: Legitimate business needs removable media, and the policy must serve them without becoming a hole. The carve-out pattern has four elements: company ownership, encryption, registration, and named roles. The field technician who images machines on customer sites genuinely needs a bootable USB drive — so the company issues it: a company-owned, hardware-encrypted drive, registered by serial number to the named technician, with read-write allowed by policy. If the drive is lost, the revocation procedure runs: the serial is blocked, the exposure is assessed (what data was on it — the answer should be 'nothing sensitive, by policy'), and a replacement is issued. Contrast with the hole version: 'field techs may use USB drives' — personal sticks, unencrypted, unregistered, unrevocable. The other common carve-outs follow the same pattern. The sales rep presenting at a client site: read-only access for presentations from a registered drive, time-bound to the trip, no write permission — the function needs read, so read is what is granted. The executive with the board presentation: same pattern, scoped to the event. The IT backup role: registered external drives, IT machines only, with the backup software's identity in the allowlist so only the backup process may write. Each carve-out states the role, the registered devices, the permitted direction (read, write, or both), the scope, and the review date — and each is reviewed on schedule, because roles change and drives get lost. Worked example: the lost-drive drill. A field tech reports their encrypted drive missing. Step one: block the serial in policy — the drive is now unusable on any company machine even if found. Step two: exposure assessment — pull the issuance record: what was provisioned on it? (Imaging tools and drivers; no customer data, per the provisioning standard.) Step three: document the incident, reissue, and review whether the provisioning standard held. The drill is the proof that the carve-out was engineered, not just permitted. Common gotcha: carve-out creep. 'The field techs have USB, why can't sales?' — because the exception was scoped to a role with a demonstrated need, and convenience is not a need. Every expansion request goes through the same four-element test. Second gotcha: encrypted-but-unregistered. Encryption without registration means you cannot revoke the specific device — the policy cannot name what it does not know. Registration is what makes the carve-out manageable.  Standardize what goes on the issued drives. The provisioning checklist should state exactly what is installed (imaging tools, drivers, the approved transfer utility), what is forbidden (customer data at rest — the drive is a transport, not storage), and how the drive is labeled and tracked (asset tag tied to the serial in the register). When a drive is lost, this standard is what makes the exposure assessment fast: 'per the provisioning standard, no customer data was on it' is an answer you can give confidently only if the standard exists and is followed. Audit the issued drives annually against the checklist.
notes.title: Legitimate carve-outs: encrypted, registered, named

notes.body: Every blocked storage attempt is a signal, and the incident walkthrough turns the signal into a verdict. The scenario: at 3:12 PM, the SOC receives a Detect alert — blocked USB mass-storage write on WORKSTATION-23, user j.chen, attempted files: \fileserver\finance\client_master.xlsx and two more. Step one is triage, and triage starts with context, not conclusions. Pull the alert's full context: device ID and whether the device is registered, the user's role and group, the exact file paths, the timestamp, and the user's recent alert history. Step two is pattern assessment: is this a first-time single attempt (possibly curiosity or a mistake) or part of a pattern (repeated attempts, multiple machines, off-hours)? Check the user's history for prior blocked storage, network, or execution alerts — a cluster across modules is far more significant than an isolated event. Step three is the user contact, handled as an interview, not an accusation: 'We saw a blocked write to a USB device on your machine this afternoon — can you walk me through what you were trying to do?' Innocent explanations are common: the new hire who did not know the policy, the manager trying to work from home, the misconfigured backup script. Step four is the verdict and it has three branches. Benign: document the explanation, provide the approved workflow (the secure file-transfer process), close the ticket. Policy violation without malice: document, retrain, and consider whether the workflow gap that drove the attempt needs fixing — repeated 'violations' often signal a broken legitimate process. Malicious or suspicious: escalate to incident response — isolate the machine, preserve the logs, image if warranted, and begin the insider-threat procedure per company policy. Step five is the feedback loop: whatever the verdict, the policy learns — a confusing block message gets rewritten, a missing legitimate workflow gets built, a new device class gets a rule. Worked example of the pattern that matters: j.chen's single blocked attempt turns out to be the third this week, each on a different workstation, each targeting finance files, each after 6 PM. No single alert is conclusive; the pattern across time, machines, and targets is the finding. That is why the walkthrough insists on history: the SOC triages patterns, not just events. Common gotcha: treating every block as an incident. Alert fatigue kills SOCs — the triage workflow exists to spend investigation effort proportional to the pattern's seriousness. Second gotcha: skipping the user interview. Logs tell you what happened; only the human tells you why — and 'why' is what separates the training opportunity from the insider case.
notes.title: Removable-media incident walkthrough

notes.body: Storage Control does not operate alone: it is one half of the data-protection pair, and the forensics it enables are what make the other half work. The pair is Storage Control plus Data Loss Prevention. Storage Control governs the path: may data move through this device, this share, this destination? It is identity-and-policy based — it knows who, what device, and where, but it does not inspect the content. DLP governs the content: is this data sensitive? It classifies — client lists, financial records, credentials, regulated data — and acts on the classification regardless of path. Together they cover the matrix: Storage Control stops the USB copy of anything, DLP stops the sensitive spreadsheet sent through an allowed channel. Neither alone is sufficient, and the operator should be able to explain the gap each leaves. The forensics side is where Storage Control pays for itself even when nothing is blocked. Every allowed and denied storage event is logged with the same schema: timestamp, user, machine, device class, device ID/serial, direction (read/write), file paths, byte counts, and the verdict. This log is the evidence chain for three questions investigators always ask. What left the machine? The write log with file paths and byte counts. When and by whom? The timestamp-user-machine triple. Was it authorized? The verdict field plus the exception register. Worked example: the post-incident timeline. A departing employee is suspected of taking client data. The investigator pulls the storage logs for the employee's last 30 days: USB writes (two blocked attempts, one allowed write to a registered drive — 400 MB, file paths listed), share access (read of the client folder, no anomalous volume), and cross-references the DLP log (no sensitive-content alerts on allowed channels). The timeline is built from logs, not from interviews — and the allowed write to the registered drive, with its file list, becomes the precise scope of the follow-up. Without the storage log, the investigation is guesswork; with it, it is accounting. Common gotcha: log retention shorter than the investigation horizon. Insider cases surface months later — if storage logs rotate after 30 days, the evidence is gone before the question is asked. Size retention to the threat model (a year is the common enterprise answer) and protect the log store itself. Second gotcha: collecting the logs but never reviewing the allowed events. Denied attempts get attention; allowed writes to registered devices are where the authorized-but-excessive data movement hides — sample them, especially around departures and role changes.

handsOnLab.brief: You will audit the listening ports on a Windows machine, classify every listener as legitimate or suspicious, and write the workstation inbound rule set that a default-deny endpoint firewall would enforce. Listener inventory to policy — the concrete skill.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: Every listening port is classified with its owning process; the rule set covers all legitimate listeners with scoped allows and denies everything else.

steps: On a Windows test machine, run Get-NetTCPConnection -State Listen | Select-Object LocalPort, OwningProcess | Sort-Object LocalPort -Unique to list listening TCP ports.
For each listening port, resolve the owning process: Get-Process -Id <PID> | Select-Object Name, Path — record process name and path.
Classify each listener: EXPECTED (system services, approved apps), REVIEW (unknown process listening — investigate), REMOVE (unneeded service — disable it).
Check UDP listeners too: Get-NetUDPEndpoint | Select-Object LocalPort, OwningProcess — classify the same way.
For each EXPECTED listener, write the firewall rule it needs: port, protocol, allowed remote scope (e.g., 'loopback only,' 'management subnet only,' 'local subnet'), and justification.
Write the default rules first: deny all inbound, deny workstation-to-workstation (SMB 445, RDP 3389, WinRM 5985/5986 between peers), then add your scoped exceptions above them.
Write the egress baseline: allow web (80/443) for approved browsers/apps, allow DNS to the company resolvers, deny-by-default egress for unknown processes.
Test one rule live: use New-NetFirewallRule to block outbound for a test process, verify with Test-NetConnection that the connection fails, then remove the rule.
Document the dynamic-ACL concept for two of your rules: under what condition does the port open (e.g., 'while the approved backup agent runs') and when does it close.
Write the troubleshooting runbook: app breaks after firewall change — identify the blocked flow (log), check the owning process, verify the destination, write the scoped exception.
Read the finished rule set as an attacker on the LAN: name which of your allowed rules you would abuse for lateral movement — then tighten the scope of the riskiest one.

notes.body: Network Control is the endpoint firewall: the deny-by-default gate for packets, just as allowlisting is the gate for code. It manages dynamic access control lists on the machine itself — ports that open and close automatically based on policy and application need — and its two headline jobs are blocking lateral movement and blocking command-and-control callbacks. Understand first why the endpoint firewall is not redundant with the network firewall. The network firewall guards segments: it sees packets, applies rules per subnet, and stops at the perimeter. The endpoint firewall guards the machine: it sees the owning process behind every connection, applies policy per process identity, and follows the laptop to the café, the home office, and the customer site. That per-process visibility is the superpower: when the network firewall logs 'blocked outbound to evil.com,' you know a packet was stopped; when the endpoint firewall logs it, you know which process, launched by whom, from what parent, tried to call out — the exact context the M07 triage workflow needs. The baseline posture has four parts. Default-deny inbound: nothing may initiate connections to the machine unless policy explicitly permits it. Default-deny workstation-to-workstation: peers do not talk to peers — SMB, RDP, and WinRM between workstations are denied, which is the containment wall from the M01 assume-breach design. Scoped exceptions with justification: every allow names the ports, the remote scope, and the business reason. Default-deny egress for unknown processes: outbound connections are gated by process identity, so malware cannot simply phone home. Worked example: the café laptop. An employee works from a coffee shop on untrusted Wi-Fi. The network firewall is irrelevant — there is none. The endpoint firewall enforces the identical policy it enforces in the office: inbound denied, peer traffic denied, the browser allowed to 80/443, the unknown process's callback denied. The policy follows the machine because it lives on the machine. Common gotcha: 'we have a network firewall, so host firewall is redundant.' The network firewall never sees the laptop at the café, never knows which process opened the connection, and cannot enforce per-process identity. They are complementary layers, not substitutes. Second gotcha: managing endpoint firewall rules like network firewall rules — static, wide, forgotten. Endpoint rules should be dynamic and scoped: open when the approved application needs the port, closed when it does not, reviewed on the same cadence as the allowlist.  The endpoint firewall also feeds the EDR's network visibility: connection logs with process attribution are among the highest-value telemetry for threat hunting, because they show which process talked to where — the question every investigation asks first. Ensure the firewall logs are forwarded to the same store as the Detect alerts so the triage workflow sees them together: the blocked lateral attempt and the process tree in one view. A firewall whose logs stay local is a witness that never testifies.
notes.title: The endpoint firewall: packets get deny-by-default too

notes.body: Static firewall rules are standing invitations: a port opened 'temporarily' in 2021 is still open, still probed, still waiting. Dynamic ACLs fix this by tying the port's state to policy and need — the port opens when the approved application requires it and closes when it does not, automatically. The concept is easiest to grasp through the contrast. Static rule: 'allow inbound TCP 8080 from anywhere, forever' — written for a demo, forgotten, discovered by a scanner within the hour, exploited within the month. Dynamic rule: 'when the approved backup agent (signed, allowlisted) starts its receive window, open TCP 8443 from the backup server's IP only; close it when the window ends' — the port exists for minutes per day, from one source, for one purpose. An attacker scanning at any other time finds nothing. The 'automatically' matters operationally: nobody files a ticket to open and close the port, so nobody forgets to close it. Worked example: the patch-management agent. Once a week it needs inbound connections from the management server to receive tasks. Static approach: port 8530 open from the management subnet permanently — a standing target that any compromised machine on that subnet can probe. Dynamic approach: the ACL opens 8530 from the single management server IP during the agent's maintenance window and closes it after. The weekly exposure drops from 168 hours to 2, from a subnet to a single IP. Multiply that across every service and the machine's attack surface becomes a flickering target instead of a lit runway. The design discipline: every allow rule states its trigger (what opens it), its scope (from whom), and its lifetime (when it closes). Rules without lifetimes are static rules with better marketing — audit for them specifically. Common gotcha: dynamic ACLs for user applications that 'need' inbound. Workstations almost never legitimately need inbound connections — the application claiming to need one is usually misconfigured (it should poll outbound) or is peer-to-peer software that does not belong on the workstation. Challenge every inbound request on a workstation; the answer is usually 'redesign the app flow,' not 'open the port.' Second gotcha: confusing dynamic with permissive. Dynamic does not mean 'opens whenever asked' — it means 'opens when policy's conditions are met.' The conditions are the control.  Give every rule a lifecycle, not just a creation. The rule record states the owner, the justification, the review date, and the condition under which it is removed (project end, decommission, migration complete). Review the rule set on the same cadence as the allowlist — quarterly at minimum — and expire rules whose justification has lapsed. Firewall rules, like allowlist entries, rot: the 'temporary' vendor access from last year's migration is still open, and the scanner will find it before you remember it.
notes.title: Dynamic ACLs: ports that open and close themselves

notes.body: Lateral movement is how one compromised machine becomes an enterprise incident, and the endpoint firewall is where you strangle it. The attacker's playbook after landing is always the same: recon the local network, authenticate to neighbors with stolen credentials, and spread. Every step of that playbook needs network paths between workstations — and the default-deny endpoint posture removes them. The three protocols to know are SMB (TCP 445, file sharing and the classic ransomware-spread vector), RDP (TCP 3389, remote desktop — the attacker's interactive console), and WinRM (TCP 5985/5986, remote management — the administrator's tool turned against them). On a workstation, inbound connections on all three from peer workstations are denied by default. Not 'monitored.' Denied. The legitimate uses get scoped exceptions, not blanket allows: IT support reaches workstations through the approved remote-access tool (which has its own policy and logging), not through open RDP; management traffic comes from the management servers, not from peers. Worked example: the 9:04 AM ransomware spread from the M01 trace. The compromised workstation begins enumerating neighbors over SMB. Each connection attempt hits the neighbor's endpoint firewall: inbound 445 from a peer workstation — denied, logged. The ransomware tries RDP with a stolen credential — inbound 3389 from a peer — denied, logged. It tries WinRM — denied, logged. Three protocols, dozens of attempts, zero successes, and each denial emits a Detect alert with the source machine identified — so the SOC knows patient zero within minutes, from the firewall logs alone. The compromised machine is now an island: it can damage itself, but it cannot recruit. That is assume breach made concrete. Common gotcha: the 'server exception' creep. 'The workstation needs SMB inbound for the scanner' — no, the scanner needs an approved, scoped path, not peer SMB. Every workstation-to-workstation exception is a lateral-movement path you built on purpose; each needs a ticket, a justification, and a review date. Second gotcha: IPv6 and alternate protocols. Denying TCP 445 while leaving the same services reachable over alternate transports is a wall with a side door — the lateral-movement policy must cover the protocol family, verified by testing from a lab machine, not by reading the rule list.  Verify the lateral-movement policy across transports, not just the famous ports. Denying TCP 445 while the same file-sharing capability is reachable over an alternate transport is a wall with a side door. Your validation should attempt the lateral movement from a lab machine using the actual techniques — not just read the rule list — and confirm each path is denied and logged. The test matrix covers the protocol families your environment actually runs, including the ones the server team forgot to mention.
notes.title: Lateral-movement prevention: strangling the spread

notes.body: If lateral movement is the attacker's expansion, the command-and-control callback is their lifeline: the compromised machine must talk to the attacker's infrastructure to receive instructions, exfiltrate data, or download stage two. Network Control cuts the lifeline with egress filtering — outbound connections gated by process identity. The rule is simple: approved processes may reach approved destinations; unknown processes reach nothing. When the M01 ransomware tried to contact its server over HTTPS at 9:04:40, the egress policy evaluated the owning process: unknown binary, no rule — denied. The callback failed before the first byte, and the attempt became a Detect alert naming the process. Note what this does to the attacker's economics. Without egress filtering, any code that runs gets a free phone line home. With it, the attacker must hijack an approved process's legitimate connection — possible (browser injection, for example) but far harder and noisier than a direct callback. The destination side matters too: even approved processes should not reach arbitrary destinations. The browser may reach the web — that is its job — but the backup agent should reach only the backup infrastructure, the updater only the vendor's endpoints. This is the network equivalent of ringfencing: the allowed app gets the network scope its function needs, nothing more. Worked example: the updater compromise scenario. An attacker compromises a software vendor and trojans the update (the supply-chain nightmare). The trojaned updater is signed by the vendor, so it passes the allowlist. It tries to phone home to the attacker's server — but the updater's network fence permits only the vendor's update endpoints. Denied, logged, alerted. The supply-chain attack dies at the egress gate because the destination was never in the approved set. This is defense in depth paying off: the layer that failed (identity) is caught by the layer that constrains behavior (network scope). Common gotcha: 'allow all outbound HTTPS' as the egress policy. HTTPS to anywhere is a callback channel with encryption — the attacker's favorite. Egress policy must be per-process and per-destination-class, or it is not a policy. Second gotcha: DNS. Egress filtering on connections without DNS filtering leaves the DNS-tunneling path open — the complete design filters both, and the M07 triage workflow treats anomalous DNS as the signal it is.  Treat DNS as part of the egress policy, not as someone else's problem. Malware that cannot open a direct connection will try DNS tunneling — encoding data in DNS queries — which sails through a firewall that filters connections but not name resolution. The complete design points endpoints at company resolvers, logs and inspects DNS queries, and treats anomalous DNS (high entropy, unusual query rates, tunneling patterns) as the detection signal it is. The M07 triage workflow should include a DNS-history check for any host under investigation.
notes.title: Blocking C2: cutting the lifeline with egress filtering

notes.body: Servers and workstations need opposite firewall postures, and applying the wrong template is a classic junior mistake. Workstations consume: they browse, they run office apps, they talk to servers. They almost never need to accept inbound connections — so workstation policy is default-deny inbound, period, with rare scoped exceptions (the approved remote-support tool, the management agent's window). Servers serve: the web server must accept inbound 80/443, the file server must accept SMB from its clients, the domain controller must accept authentication traffic. Server policy is therefore scoped-allow inbound per service: each listening service gets a rule naming the ports, the permitted sources, and nothing else. The discipline is identical — least privilege — but the shape inverts: workstations deny nearly everything inbound, servers allow precisely what they serve. Worked example: the mis-templated web server. A new web server accidentally receives the workstation firewall template: inbound 80/443 denied, and the site is down. The fix is not 'open everything' — it is the server template: allow TCP 80/443 inbound from the load balancer and the monitoring hosts, allow admin ports (RDP/SSH/WinRM) from the jump host only, deny everything else, and deny server-to-workstation initiation except the management paths. Conversely, the workstation that someone 'fixed' by applying the server template now accepts inbound SMB from the subnet — a lateral-movement gift. The rule: the template follows the role, and role changes trigger policy review. The management-plane design deserves its own attention: servers need administration, and administration needs paths. The correct pattern is the jump host (or privileged access workstation): admin protocols are permitted only from the hardened jump host to the servers, never from workstations to servers directly, and never between servers except the specific service traffic. This turns the admin path into a chokepoint you can monitor, log, and protect — instead of a mesh of standing admin access. Common gotcha: 'the server needs internet access' as a blanket statement. Servers need specific destinations (update servers, vendor endpoints, monitoring) — each named, each scoped. A server with unrestricted outbound is a C2 launchpad waiting for a compromise. Second gotcha: forgetting the server's own workstation-like behaviors. Servers browse the web for 'quick downloads' — they should not; software comes through the deployment pipeline. The server egress policy should be as tight as its inbound.  Harden the jump host like the crown jewel it is: no internet browsing, no email, allowlisted applications only, every session logged, and access requiring phishing-resistant authentication. A compromised jump host inherits its administrative reach — the chokepoint becomes the prize. Review who holds jump-host access quarterly, because the list grows silently and every name on it is a path to every server. The jump host is the one machine where 'inconvenient security' is the entire point.
notes.title: Server vs workstation: opposite postures, same discipline

notes.body: Firewall policy is the number-one suspect when 'the app worked yesterday,' so the troubleshooting discipline must be structured — random rule-toggling creates holes. The triage order is fixed. Step one: identify the blocked flow. Pull the firewall log for the timeframe: source, destination, port, protocol, direction, and — the endpoint firewall's gift — the owning process. Most 'mystery outages' end here: the log names the exact denied connection. Step two: check the owning process against policy. Is this process approved? Is it the legitimate application or something wearing its name? Verify identity (hash, certificate, path) before touching any rule — opening a port for malware because 'the app needed it' is the classic self-inflicted breach. Step three: verify the destination's legitimacy. Is this the vendor's real update endpoint or a lookalike? Check DNS, check the vendor's published endpoints, be suspicious of anything newly registered. Step four: write the scoped exception. The exception names the process, the ports, the destination scope, and the justification — and it goes above the deny rules, documented, with a review date. Never 'allow all outbound for the app to see if that fixes it' — that is not troubleshooting, it is surrender. Worked example: Monday 9 AM, the accounting package cannot reach its cloud service after a weekend policy push. Triage: the firewall log shows denied outbound TCP 443 from AcctApp.exe to 203.0.113.45. Process check: AcctApp.exe is allowlisted, signed by the vendor, parent chain clean. Destination check: 203.0.113.45 is in the vendor's published endpoint list (verified via the vendor's docs, not the user's word). Verdict: the weekend policy tightened egress without the vendor's endpoint range. Fix: scoped exception — AcctApp.exe may reach the vendor's published endpoint range on 443, documented with the ticket, review in 90 days. Total downtime: 20 minutes, because the triage order went straight to the evidence. Common gotcha: the 'temporary allow-any' that becomes permanent. Every troubleshooter is tempted; the discipline is writing the scoped rule even under pressure, because the emergency you fix today with a hole becomes the incident you investigate next quarter. Second gotcha: troubleshooting the firewall when the problem is DNS, the proxy, or the application itself. The firewall log is step one precisely because it tells you in seconds whether the firewall is even involved — if there is no denied flow, look elsewhere.  Record every exception in the change system with the same five fields as the allowlist: requester, justification, scope, expiry, approver. The firewall exception register is audited alongside the others, and 'temporary vendor access' without an expiry is the rule most likely to be found open two years later. When the auditor asks why port X is open to subnet Y, the register should answer in one lookup — that is the difference between a managed firewall and a collection of rules.

notes.body: ThreatLocker Detect is the module that turns prevention into intelligence: it alerts on the indicators of compromise that the other modules blocked. Every denied execution, every fenced child-process spawn, every blocked USB write and every denied lateral connection emits an alert carrying the full context — the process, its parent chain, the user, the machine, the timestamp, and exactly which policy said no. Understand why this inverts the traditional SOC experience. In a detection-first world (classic EDR), the sensor watches the attack run and tries to recognize malice in progress: behavioral analytics, machine-learning scores, threat-intel matches. The alert says, in effect, 'something looks 73% malicious, please investigate while it continues.' Analysts drown in probabilistic leads, most benign, and the true positives arrive while the damage is underway. In the prevention-first world, the enforcement already stopped the attempt — the alert says 'this specific action was attempted and denied,' which is a statement of fact, not a probability. A blocked child-process spawn from Word at 9:02 AM is not 73% suspicious; it is an attempted attack step, caught red-handed, with the evidence attached. This is why prevention-first alerts are higher fidelity: the enforcement decision pre-filters the noise. The benign application that behaves normally never triggers; the malicious step triggers by attempting the forbidden. Worked example: compare the two SOC mornings. Detection-first SOC: 400 alerts overnight — 380 benign (updaters, admin tools, user oddities scored as suspicious), 15 duplicates, 5 worth reading, 1 real. The analyst's morning is triage-as-archaeology, and the real one is buried. Prevention-first SOC: 12 alerts overnight — each a blocked action with full context. The analyst reads 12 factual events, clears 8 as benign-with-reason (stale hash rule, approved updater), and escalates 4 with evidence. Same company, same threats, radically different signal-to-noise — because the blocks did the filtering. Common gotcha: 'fewer alerts means less visibility.' The opposite: the prevented attempts are the highest-value visibility you can get — malice confirmed at the attempt stage, before damage. The SOC's job shifts from finding needles in haystacks to judging 12 needles, which is a job humans can actually do well. Second gotcha: treating Detect as 'just logging.' The alert pipeline — severity, routing, SLA, runbook — is what makes the blocks operationally useful. Blocks without triage are security theater with receipts.  Design the alert routing before the alerts arrive. Critical-severity alerts page the on-call analyst; high-severity alerts land in the priority queue with a one-hour triage SLA; everything else flows to the standard queue. Route by asset criticality too — the domain controller's medium is the kiosk's critical. And build the queue dashboards around the runbook's verdicts, not raw counts: 'alerts triaged to incident this week' is a security metric, 'total alerts' is just weather. The routing design is what keeps the 2 AM alert from waiting until 9 AM.
notes.title: What Detect is: the block becomes the signal

notes.body: Every alert gets the same five-input triage, in the same order, because consistency is what makes a SOC defensible and auditable. Input one: severity. The alert's initial severity comes from the policy that fired and the action blocked — a blocked unsigned execution in temp is higher severity than a blocked updater with a stale rule. Severity sets the SLA clock: critical starts triage in minutes, medium in hours. Input two: asset criticality. The same block on the domain controller and on a kiosk are different events — know your crown jewels (finance workstations, servers, executive machines, IT admin boxes) and weight accordingly. Input three: user and role context. Who was at the keyboard? The finance user's blocked macro at 9 AM during month-end reads differently than the same block on a service account at 3 AM. Check whether the user is where they should be, doing what they should do. Input four: the blocked action's details. Read the actual event: which process, which parent, what was attempted, what was the target, what arguments were passed? Encoded PowerShell arguments are a different universe from a missing file path. Input five: pattern history. Has this user, this machine, this process generated similar alerts? One blocked USB write is curiosity; three in a week across machines is intent. The verdict has three branches. Benign: the block was correct but harmless — stale rule, approved tool, user error. Action: fix the rule or educate the user, document, close. Policy violation without malice: the user tried to bypass policy for convenience. Action: document, retrain, check whether a broken legitimate workflow drove it. Incident: real attack attempt or suspicious pattern. Action: escalate per the runbook — isolate, preserve, investigate. Worked example: the 9:02 AM alert from M01. Severity: high (blocked child-process spawn, encoded args). Asset: accounting workstation (crown jewel — finance data). User: m.reyes, finance, at her desk at 9 AM (context fits). Action details: winword.exe → powershell.exe, encoded command line (malicious pattern). History: first alert for this user/machine. Verdict: incident — isolate ACCOUNTING-07, preserve the logs, escalate to IR. The triage took the five inputs in order and produced a defensible verdict in minutes. Common gotcha: verdict before context. Reading the alert title and deciding 'it's just the updater' without checking the arguments is how real intrusions get closed as benign. The workflow's order exists to prevent exactly this. Second gotcha: severity as destiny. Initial severity starts the clock; the triage determines the verdict. A 'medium' alert with a malicious pattern history becomes an incident — let the inputs move the verdict.
notes.title: The alert triage workflow: five inputs, three verdicts

notes.body: Prevention-first versus detection-first is the architectural debate underneath every EDR conversation, and you should be able to argue it from the operator's chair. Detection-first (traditional EDR) assumes the attack will run: the sensor monitors process behavior, network flows, and file activity, and tries to recognize malice while it executes. Its strengths are real: it catches fileless attacks, it sees the techniques that prevention misses, and its telemetry is invaluable for hunting. Its structural weakness is time: recognition happens during or after the malicious action, so the SOC races the attacker — and the attacker only needs to be faster than the analyst's queue. Prevention-first (Detect's model) assumes the attempt can be stopped: the policy denies the malicious action before it executes, and the denial becomes the alert. Its strength is the timeline: the SOC starts at the attempt stage, with the attack already dead. Its honest limitation is coverage: prevention stops what policy forbids, so novel techniques outside the fenced behaviors still need detection — which is why the mature design is prevention-first with detection depth, not prevention-only. The dwell-time argument needs care: you will hear claims about average attacker dwell times, but do not quote numbers you cannot source. The structural argument needs no numbers: an alert at the attempt stage is earlier than an alert at the damage stage, by construction. Worked example: the same intrusion against both architectures. Detection-first: the attacker lands, the EDR scores the behavior, an alert fires mid-encryption, the analyst starts triage while files encrypt — the race is on. Prevention-first: the attacker's first malicious step (the child-process spawn) is denied at 9:02:14, the alert fires at 9:02:15 with the attack dead — the analyst triages a corpse, calmly, with full evidence. The incident still gets investigated (how did the document arrive? are there others?), but nobody is racing encryption. Common gotcha: presenting prevention-first as making detection obsolete. It does not — it changes detection's job from 'catch the attack in progress' to 'judge the attempts and hunt what policy missed.' The SOC still hunts; it just hunts from a position of already having stopped the bleeding. Second gotcha: assuming prevented means uninteresting. The blocked attempt is the highest-quality threat intelligence the company produces — it names the attacker's current tools, targets, and timing. Feed it to the threat-intel process, not just the ticket queue.  Close the loop between triage and prevention. Every incident verdict should produce at least one candidate policy improvement: a new ringfence behavior to deny, an allowlist rule to tighten, an egress destination to remove. Track these as follow-up tickets owned by the policy team, not as informal suggestions — the SOC sees the attacks, the policy team owns the gates, and the feedback ticket is the bridge. A SOC whose findings never change policy is an expensive observation deck.
notes.title: Detect vs traditional EDR: prevention-first vs detection-first

notes.body: When an alert exceeds your authority, evidence, or expertise, it goes to the managed detection and response provider — and the quality of your handoff determines the quality of their response. The MDR handoff is a package, not a forward: it contains everything the MDR analyst needs to act without re-doing your triage. The package has six fields. Who/what/when/where: user, machine, timestamp, alert ID — the identifiers that let them pull their own telemetry. The blocked action with full context: which policy fired, which process and parent, what was attempted, the arguments or targets — the factual core. What you already checked: the triage steps completed and their results — 'verified the binary hash against the vendor's published value: no match' saves them an hour. Your verdict and reasoning: incident-suspected, with the two or three facts that drove it — they will form their own judgment, but they deserve your read. The evidence links: alert IDs, log locations, ticket numbers — no 'the logs are somewhere in the console.' The specific ask: what you need — 'please confirm whether this hash appears in your wider telemetry' or 'requesting containment approval for these three machines.' Worked example: the 2 AM unknown-process alert. Handoff: 'ACCOUNTING-07, user m.reyes, 02:14 — blocked outbound HTTPS from update_svc.exe (unsigned, temp path) to unlisted destination. Checked: binary not in allowlist, hash unknown to reputation, parent is a scheduled task created yesterday, user states they were asleep. Verdict: suspected intrusion — the process identity, timing, and persistence mechanism all indicate malice. Evidence: alert DET-8841, process tree in ticket IR-2203. Ask: please check your telemetry for this hash across our estate and advise on containment scope.' That handoff gets action in minutes; a bare alert forward gets questions for an hour. The escalation criteria in your runbook define when the handoff happens: suspected incidents go immediately, pattern-level suspicions go with the pattern summary, and anything involving crown-jewel assets goes faster. Common gotcha: handoff as abdication. The MDR extends your team; it does not replace your triage. A handoff that says 'please investigate this alert' with no context is a confession that you skipped the workflow. Second gotcha: no feedback loop. When the MDR closes the case, their verdict comes back into your runbook — the tuning, the new detection, the lessons learned. Handoffs without feedback are a treadmill.  Set handoff SLAs with the MDR provider in the contract, not in the crisis. Define the severity-to-response-time mapping, the escalation path when the SLA is missed, and the format of the verdict that comes back — because the feedback is what tunes your runbook. Review the handoff quality quarterly with real tickets: were the packages complete, were the asks specific, did the verdicts come back in time to act? The MDR relationship is operated like any vendor relationship: measured, reviewed, and improved.
notes.title: MDR handoff: packaging the alert for action

notes.body: The runbook is the module's deliverable because it makes triage a property of the organization, not of whoever happens to be on shift. A Detect alert runbook has six parts, and you will write one in the lab. Part one: the trigger — which alert, from which policy, in plain language ('blocked child-process spawn from an Office application'). Part two: default severity and SLA — how fast triage starts. Part three: context to gather — the exact fields and where to find them (process, parent chain, user, machine, time, the user's alert history). Part four: triage steps in order — the five-input workflow from this module, written as checkable steps. Part five: verdict branches — what benign, violation, and incident each look like for this alert type, with two or three concrete examples per branch. Part six: escalation criteria — exactly when this goes to the MDR, to IR, or to management, with the handoff package template attached. Worked example: the runbook section for 'blocked USB mass-storage write.' Trigger: storage policy deny on removable-media write. Severity: medium default; high if finance/engineering asset or repeat pattern. Context: device ID and registration status, user and role, file paths and byte counts, the user's 30-day alert history. Triage: check registration (registered drive blocked = possible stale exception), check the files (sensitive paths raise severity), check history (pattern = intent). Verdicts: benign — new hire unaware of policy, first occurrence, non-sensitive files (action: educate, close). Violation — repeat attempts, no malice indicators (action: retrain, check workflow gap). Incident — sensitive targets, multiple machines, off-hours, or combined with other module alerts (action: isolate, preserve, escalate to IR). Escalation: any incident-verdict goes to IR immediately; any pattern of three-plus attempts goes to the security lead same-day. The runbook also carries the tuning section: after 30 days, which alerts proved benign-by-pattern get documented suppressions — each suppression naming the pattern, the owner, and the review date. Common gotcha: the runbook as shelfware. A runbook nobody opens during triage is documentation theater — it must be short enough to use mid-incident, linked from the alert itself, and updated every time a triage teaches something new. Second gotcha: verdict branches without examples. 'Use your judgment' is not a branch — the examples are what let a junior analyst triage like a senior at 3 AM.  Version the runbook and review it on a schedule — monthly for the active sections, quarterly cover to cover. Every triage that teaches something new produces a runbook update: a new example in a verdict branch, a tightened escalation criterion, a new tuning rule. Keep a changelog so analysts can see what changed and why; a runbook that silently mutates loses trust. The review meeting is short when the changelog does the talking: what did we learn, what did we change, what needs re-tuning.
notes.title: Building the Detect alert runbook

notes.body: Alert fatigue is the SOC's chronic illness: too many alerts, too little signal, analysts skimming, real incidents missed in the noise. Prevention-first architectures start with an advantage — the blocks pre-filter — but the advantage erodes without tuning discipline. The tuning program has four parts. Baselining: for the first 30-60 days, every alert type gets its benign rate measured — which alerts fire, how often, and what fraction prove benign. You cannot tune what you have not measured. Documented suppression: benign-by-pattern alerts get suppression rules — but every suppression is a written decision naming the pattern, the evidence it is benign, the owner, and the review date. 'We suppressed updater blocks' is blindness; 'we suppress blocks where the binary is vendor-signed, the hash matches the vendor's published value, and the parent is the approved updater — owner: SOC lead, review: quarterly' is tuning. Anomaly preservation: suppressions target known-benign patterns only — anything novel, anything from a new process, anything off-pattern still fires. The day the 'known-benign' updater behaves differently is the day you want the alert. Review cadence: suppressions expire and are re-justified on schedule, because vendors get compromised and benign patterns change. Worked example: the updater-block tuning. Week one: 40 alerts — 'blocked execution of vendor updater, hash mismatch.' Triage shows the vendor rotated their signing certificate; the binaries are legitimate. Suppression written: allow the new certificate for the updater product, scoped, owner named, 90-day review. Alerts drop to zero for this pattern — legitimately, because the policy now reflects reality. Contrast with the lazy version: 'suppress all updater alerts' — which would also suppress the trojaned updater next quarter. The case walkthrough that ties the module together: the full M01 attack as a Detect story. 9:02:14 — blocked child-process spawn (winword.exe → powershell.exe), severity high, full context attached. 9:02:15 — blocked file write to temp. 9:02:16 — blocked unknown execution. Three alerts, one incident, one timeline: the SOC sees the attacker's playbook in the order it was attempted, each step already dead. The analyst's job is verdict and scope (how did the document arrive? any other recipients?), not a race against encryption. That is the prevention-first SOC: fewer alerts, each factual, triaged at the attempt stage. Common gotcha: tuning by volume instead of by pattern. 'Reduce alerts by 50%' as a goal produces blind suppressions; 'every alert type has a measured benign rate and a documented disposition' produces a tuned SOC. Second gotcha: the hero analyst who 'just knows.' Institutionalize the knowledge in the runbook — heroes go on vacation, runbooks do not.

handsOnLab.brief: You will audit a Windows machine's Defender configuration with PowerShell, harden it to a written baseline, export the baseline, and build a drift-check script that compares any machine against it. Baseline-as-code for the endpoint security stack.
handsOnLab.checkpoint: The baseline document lists every setting with its value and rationale; the drift script runs clean against the hardened machine and flags a deliberately introduced deviation.
handsOnLab.deliverable: defender-baseline.md plus Test-DefenderDrift.ps1 — the standard and the checker.
steps: On a Windows test machine, run Get-MpPreference and record the current values of: DisableRealtimeMonitoring, MAPSReporting (cloud protection), DisableTamperProtection, and ExclusionPath/ExclusionProcess.
Run Get-MpComputerStatus and record: RealTimeProtectionEnabled, AntivirusEnabled, TamperProtectionSource, and the signature ages (AntivirusSignatureAge).
Write defender-baseline.md: for each setting, the required value and a one-line rationale (e.g., 'MAPSReporting=2 Advanced: unknown files get cloud verdicts').
Harden the test machine to your baseline with Set-MpPreference (e.g., Set-MpPreference -MAPSReporting Advanced -SubmitSamplesConsent SendSafeSamplesMap); record each command.
Review the exclusion lists: for every existing exclusion, write the justification or remove it — document which you removed and why.
Write Test-DefenderDrift.ps1: a script that reads Get-MpPreference, compares each value to your baseline hashtable, and outputs PASS/FAIL per setting with the actual vs expected values.
Run the drift script against the hardened machine — confirm all PASS.
Introduce a deliberate deviation (add a test exclusion path), re-run the script, and confirm it flags the deviation — then remove the test exclusion.
Add an exclusion-hygiene section to the baseline doc: the required fields for every exclusion (requester, justification, scope, expiry, reviewer).
Write the rollout note: pilot ring (IT first), one-week monitoring (blocks, performance complaints), expansion criteria, and rollback trigger.
Read the finished baseline as the auditor from the drill: confirm you can prove consistent configuration from the document plus a drift-report run.

notes.body: Microsoft Defender is on every Windows endpoint you will manage, which makes its configuration one of the highest-leverage baselines in the environment — and one of the most commonly left to rot. Without centralized management, Defender configuration decays into folklore: real-time protection disabled on 'that one machine that was slow,' exclusions added by whoever had admin that day for reasons nobody remembers, cloud protection off because someone clicked through a prompt in 2022. Each machine becomes its own policy, the 'standard' exists only in a document nobody follows, and the auditor's sample inevitably finds the worst one. Configuration Manager fixes this by treating Defender settings as code: one baseline, defined centrally, pushed to every machine, with the actual configuration continuously compared against the intended. The baseline covers the protection stack. Real-time protection: the always-on guard that scans files on access — the setting that must never be off, because everything else assumes it is on. Cloud-delivered protection: unknown files get verdicts from Microsoft's cloud telemetry in seconds — the layer that covers what local signatures have never seen. Tamper protection: locks the settings themselves so malware (or a compromised admin) cannot silently disable the guard. Automatic sample submission and signature update cadence: the freshness of the intelligence. Exclusions: the deliberate blind spots, each justified (more on those below). Worked example: the 'slow machine' incident. A user complains their workstation is slow; a well-meaning tech disables real-time protection 'temporarily.' Six months later the machine is patient zero in a malware incident — and nobody knows protection was off because no central system compared actual to intended. With centralized management, the drift report flags the machine within the check cycle: 'WORKSTATION-14: real-time protection disabled, baseline requires enabled.' The operator re-pushes the baseline, investigates the performance complaint properly (which turns out to be a failing disk), and the hole closes in hours instead of being discovered during incident response. Common gotcha: assuming defaults are the baseline. Defender's out-of-box settings are reasonable but they are not your policy — cloud protection levels, sample submission consent, exclusion lists, and tamper protection all need deliberate decisions recorded in the baseline document. Second gotcha: managing the baseline but not the drift. A pushed policy that nobody verifies is a wish; the continuous comparison — intended vs actual, machine by machine — is what makes it a control.  Deliver the baseline through the same channel as the rest of your configuration management — Group Policy for domain-joined machines, the MDM for the mobile fleet — so the baseline inherits the existing change control, targeting, and reporting. Do not manage Defender through a side channel with its own console and its own process; the side channel becomes the thing everyone forgets during incidents. One configuration pipeline, one change record, one place to check what was pushed and when.
notes.title: Why Defender configuration needs central management

notes.body: The baseline is a document before it is a deployment: every setting, its required value, and the one-line rationale. Write it like an auditor will read it, because one will. The protection core: real-time protection enabled — the always-on scanning at file access, the non-negotiable. Cloud-delivered protection set to the advanced level — unknown executables get cloud verdicts within seconds, which is the only scalable answer to never-before-seen files. Tamper protection enabled — settings locked against modification by malware or unauthorized admins; verify it is actually on, because it is the setting that protects the settings. Behavior monitoring enabled — the heuristic layer that catches malicious actions rather than just malicious files. Signature updates automatic on the fastest practical cadence — stale intelligence is a choice to be less protected. Sample submission configured per company policy — automatic submission of safe samples improves the collective verdicts; the policy decision is what may leave the building. Then the platform settings: scheduled scan cadence (the weekly full scan that catches what real-time missed), scan scope (all drives, including removable — the M05 device policy and the scan policy must agree), and threat-default-actions (what happens on detection: quarantine first, never 'allow'). Worked example: the baseline document excerpt. 'MAPSReporting = Advanced. Rationale: unknown files receive cloud verdicts in seconds; local-only verdicts miss zero-day samples. Risk accepted: file metadata leaves the machine per the data-handling policy §4.2.' Every setting gets this treatment — value plus rationale plus the risk decision. The document is versioned, change-controlled, and reviewed quarterly: baseline changes go through the same change process as firewall rules, because they are the same class of control. Common gotcha: the 'recommended' trap. Vendor 'recommended' settings are a starting point, not your baseline — your baseline reflects your threat model, your data-handling policy, and your operational capacity. If your SOC cannot handle the alert volume of the most aggressive heuristic level, the honest baseline is the level you will actually operate, documented as such. Second gotcha: baseline without exception process. Legitimate needs will conflict with the baseline (the developer tool that the heuristics hate) — the baseline document must name the exception process, or people will bypass the baseline silently. The exclusion discipline below is that process.  Watch the interplay between scan settings and exclusions: aggressive heuristic levels plus a broad exclusion list is the worst combination — maximum noise where you look, blindness where you do not. Tune them as a pair: set the protection level you can actually operate (alerts your SOC will triage, performance your users will tolerate), then keep the exclusion list as short as the narrowness ladder allows. The baseline document should record both decisions together with the reasoning, so the next operator understands the balance rather than inheriting half of it.
notes.title: The baseline: every setting, its value, its rationale

notes.body: Exclusions are deliberate blind spots: places Defender is told not to look. Every exclusion ever added was added for a reason that felt good at the time — and every major Defender bypass story involves an exclusion. The discipline is therefore strict: no exclusion without the five fields. Requester: who asked, so there is a human attached. Justification: the specific technical reason — 'the build agent's output directory triggers heuristic false positives on every compile, verified with the vendor' is a justification; 'it was slow' is not. Scope: the narrowest possible — a process exclusion for the specific binary beats a path exclusion for the folder, which beats excluding the drive. Expiry and review: exclusions rot as software changes, so each gets a review date (90 days is the working default). Approver: someone who understands what 'Defender will not look here' means. The exclusion types map to the narrowness ladder. Process exclusions: Defender skips files opened by the named process — the narrowest, preferred for build tools and backup agents. Path exclusions: Defender skips the folder — broader, acceptable for vendor-verified application directories, never for user-writable locations. Extension exclusions: Defender skips file types — the broadest per-file-type, justified only for large non-executable data (and never for executables). File-type and the classic mistake: excluding .exe or script extensions 'for performance' is functionally disabling protection for the most dangerous files. Worked example: the build-server exclusion request. The dev team reports 40-minute builds with Defender scanning the output directory. The operator verifies: the directory contains only build artifacts, the build tool is allowlisted and signed, the false positives are documented. Exclusion written: process exclusion for buildtool.exe plus path exclusion for D:\build-output\ — scoped to the build servers, requested by the dev lead, approved by security, 90-day review, ticket BUILD-118. The builds drop to 12 minutes; the exclusion is fenced to machines whose entire purpose is building, and the review will catch it if the tool changes. Contrast with the hole version: 'exclude D:\ from scanning on all machines because someone's build was slow once.' Common gotcha: temp-folder exclusions. Excluding temp, downloads, or the user's profile from scanning blinds Defender exactly where malware lands — these are the last places that should ever be excluded, and any request for them is a red flag to investigate, not a ticket to approve. Second gotcha: exclusion without compensating control. A broad-but-necessary exclusion (the legacy app's folder) should trigger a question: what covers this blind spot instead? The allowlist still gates execution there; the ringfence still constrains behavior — document the compensating controls in the exclusion record.
notes.title: Exclusions: deliberate blind spots, strict discipline

notes.body: Configuration drift is entropy applied to security settings: the slow divergence between what the baseline says and what the machines actually run. It has a dozen causes — the tech who 'temporarily' changed a setting, the GPO that stopped applying after an OU move, the laptop that missed three policy cycles, the admin who added an exclusion directly on the machine and never told anyone. Drift detection is the continuous comparison of intended vs actual, machine by machine, setting by setting, and it is what separates managed from unmanaged. The mechanics are straightforward: the manager collects each machine's effective Defender configuration on a schedule, compares it to the baseline, and reports every divergence with the machine name, the setting, the expected value, and the actual value. The operator's workflow on a drift report is fixed: verify the divergence is real (not a reporting artifact), determine the cause (authorized change? rogue change? policy failure?), remediate (re-push the baseline or process the authorized change through change control), and document. Worked example: the Tuesday drift report. 197 machines clean. WORKSTATION-14: real-time protection disabled (expected: enabled). WORKSTATION-31: exclusion path C:\tools\ added (not in baseline). SERVER-02: cloud protection set to basic (expected: advanced). Three divergences, three investigations. WORKSTATION-14: the 'slow machine' tech from this module's first note — remediation: re-push baseline, address the actual performance cause, counsel the tech on the change process. WORKSTATION-31: an admin added it directly during an incident last week and forgot — remediation: process it as a proper exclusion request or remove it. SERVER-02: the OU move broke GPO inheritance — remediation: fix the OU linking, re-push, verify. The report turned three silent holes into three closed tickets in one morning. That is the entire value proposition. Common gotcha: drift reports nobody reads. The report must have an owner, a review cadence (daily for critical settings, weekly for the full baseline), and an SLA for remediation — an unread drift report is the same as no drift detection. Second gotcha: treating drift as purely technical. Repeated drift from the same team is a process signal: either the baseline is wrong for their workflow (fix the baseline or grant a proper exception) or the change discipline is broken (fix the discipline). The drift pattern tells you which.  Automate the drift check — a scheduled task or pipeline job that runs the comparison, files the report, and opens tickets for divergences above the threshold. Manual drift review works for twenty machines and collapses at two hundred; the automation is what makes the control scale. Keep the automation's own health monitored: a drift job that silently stopped running is worse than no job, because the dashboard still shows the last green report. Monitor the monitor.
notes.title: Drift detection: intended vs actual, continuously

notes.body: Defender and allowlisting are complementary, not competing — and the operator must be fluent in which question each answers. Defender asks 'is this file malicious?' It scans content against signatures, heuristics, and cloud verdicts, and it acts on malice found. Allowlisting asks 'may this code execute?' It checks identity against policy and acts on the absence of approval. A signed-but-malicious file can pass the allowlist and be caught by Defender's behavior monitoring; an unknown-but-benign tool can be blocked by the allowlist while Defender finds nothing wrong with it. Neither is sufficient alone; together they cover the matrix of known/unknown crossed with malicious/benign. The operational consequence is that both need management, and the management must agree. The exclusion list and the allowlist are the two documents most likely to contradict each other: an application excluded from Defender scanning but blocked by the allowlist (confused users, mysterious failures), or an application allowlisted but hammered by Defender heuristics (performance complaints, pressure for bad exclusions). The centralized console's value is making both visible in one place so the contradictions surface before the tickets do. Worked example: the backup agent. It is allowlisted (signed, approved, needed on all servers). Defender's behavior monitoring flags its volume-shadow-copy activity as ransomware-like. Without central visibility, the server team demands a broad exclusion and the security team refuses — stalemate. With both policies visible, the operator writes the precise fix: a process exclusion for the backup agent's binary (narrowest scope), documented with the vendor's confirmation that the behavior is expected, 90-day review — and notes the compensating control (the agent is allowlisted and ringfenced, so the blind spot is fenced). The rollout discipline for baseline changes mirrors every rollout in this course: pilot ring (IT and a friendly department), one-week monitoring of blocks, detections, and performance complaints, staged expansion, and a rollback trigger defined before the push ('if legitimate blocks exceed N per day, we revert and review'). Common gotcha: changing the baseline and the allowlist in the same window. When the backup breaks on Monday, you need to know which change did it — sequence the rollouts, never stack them. Second gotcha: the 'Defender found nothing, so we're fine' fallacy in reverse. Defender finding nothing means no known malice detected; the allowlist blocking an unknown means no approval exists. Both signals matter, and the M07 triage workflow treats them as the complementary evidence they are.  Keep one exceptions register, not three. The allowlist exceptions, the Defender exclusions, and the firewall exceptions all describe deliberate blind spots or openings — review them together quarterly, because a machine with an exclusion in all three is a machine with no controls left. The joint review is where the dangerous combinations surface: the unsigned tool that is allowlisted, excluded from scanning, and granted firewall exceptions is a policy decision that deserves executive visibility, not three separate tickets nobody connected.
notes.title: Defense in depth: Defender plus allowlisting, managed together

notes.body: The rollout and the audit are where this module meets the real world. Rollout first: a Defender baseline change is a change to the security posture of every machine, so it gets the staged discipline. Ring zero: the security team's own machines — if the baseline breaks the people who wrote it, better to learn at 10 AM than company-wide at 9. Ring one: IT and a pilot department, one week, with explicit monitoring — detection counts, block rates, helpdesk tickets mentioning slowness or blocks, and the drift report confirming the baseline actually applied. Ring two: the rest, in waves, with the rollback trigger armed: a defined threshold of legitimate-impact tickets pauses the rollout for review. The emergency brake is the baseline versioning: every push is versioned, so rollback is 're-push the previous version,' not archaeology. Then the audit story, because this module exists partly to make audits boring. The auditor asks: 'prove consistent antivirus configuration across the estate.' The unmanaged answer is a scramble — screenshots from three machines, a policy document of uncertain age, and hope. The managed answer is two artifacts: the versioned baseline document (every setting, value, rationale, change history) and the latest drift report (intended vs actual, machine by machine, divergences remediated with tickets). The auditor samples five machines; all five match the baseline; the two divergences from last month show remediation tickets. That is a control, demonstrated. Worked example: the quarterly review meeting. The operator brings three things: the drift trend (divergences per week, falling since the OU fix), the exclusion register (12 active exclusions, 3 due for review, 2 removed last quarter), and the proposed baseline change (stricter cloud-protection level, with pilot results from ring zero showing no legitimate impact). The meeting takes 20 minutes because the artifacts do the talking. This is what 'managed' looks like from the outside: boring, evidenced, continuous. Common gotcha: the big-bang baseline push. 'We're pushing the new baseline to all 200 machines Friday at 5' is how you spend the weekend rolling back. Staged, monitored, reversible — the discipline is the same in M02, M03, and here, because the failure mode (breaking the business at scale) is the same. Second gotcha: audit theater — a beautiful baseline document with no drift detection behind it. The document claims; the drift report proves. Bring both, always.  Run the quarterly review as a business meeting, not a technical deep dive. The operator brings the drift trend, the exclusion register with upcoming reviews, and one proposed change with pilot data — the leadership brings the risk appetite. Twenty minutes, three artifacts, decisions recorded. This cadence is what keeps the baseline a living standard instead of a document: the review is where stale exclusions die, where drift patterns get resourced, and where the next quarter's hardening is agreed. Boring, regular, effective.
notes.title: Rollout rings and the boring audit

It gets rapid verdicts on unknown files from cloud telemetry — covering what local signatures have never seen

summary: Defender is on every Windows machine you will manage — its configuration is a high-leverage baseline that decays without central management. This module covers the full baseline (real-time, cloud, tamper protection), the strict exclusion discipline, continuous drift detection, defense-in-depth with allowlisting, and the rollout and audit practices that make compliance boring.
